title: 21.13.24 Newton bodies
section: 21.13 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Let $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ be the set of $T_ c$-invariant functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Definition 21.13.25 . D7E78CFDB281 A function $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ can be written as \[  \varphi |_{T(\mathbb {C})}=\operatorname{Trop}^*f  \] for some unique function $f\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$. Then we define $F_{\varphi }\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ as follows: E09FCEF2675C 21.13.26 \begin{equation}  F_{\varphi }=F_{\theta }+f. \end{equation} Observe that $F_{\varphi }$ is a convex function and takes finite values by 21.12.7 . In particular, $f$ is also real-valued. Once $D$ and $h$ are fixed, $F_{\varphi }$ is well-defined up to a constant since $F_{\theta }$ is. Definition 21.13.27 . 22C597E4DEB2 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$, we define its Newton body as \[  \Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\coloneqq \overline{\nabla F_{\varphi }(N_{\mathbb {R}})}\subseteq M_{\mathbb {R}}.  \] Here the gradient is understood in the sense of Alexandrov, see definition 21.11.30 for the details. Note that $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )$ is independent of the choice of $s_ D$. The Newton body $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )$ depends on the choice of $D$, not only on the associated line bundle $L$: A different choice of $D$ inducing the same line bundle corresponds to a translation of $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )$. We will see in a while (theorem 21.13.39 ) that once $D$ is fixed $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )$ depends only on the current $\theta _{\varphi }$. Hence, the choice of $h$ is irrelevant. For the moment, it is not clear if $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\subseteq P_ D$ or not. We shall prove this result using the theory of partial Okounkov bodies in the next section. Proposition 21.13.28 . 49A9A66B3A4D Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$. Then 04F5C34B36CA 21.13.29 \begin{equation}  \operatorname{Trop}_* \left(\theta |_{T(\mathbb {C})}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi |_{T(\mathbb {C})} \right)^ n=\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}\left(F_{\varphi }\right). \end{equation} In particular, 5FCC3FDF4C75 21.13.30 \begin{equation}  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n =n! \operatorname{vol}\Delta (\theta ,\varphi ) \end{equation} Proof. Let $F_0$ be a smooth convex function on $N_{\mathbb {R}}$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\operatorname{Trop}^* F_0$ can be extended to a Kähler form on $X$. For example, Guillemin's construction ( 21.12.9 ) with respect to a suitable Delzant polytope gives such an example. Write $\omega $ for a Kähler form on $X$ extending $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\operatorname{Trop}^*F_0$. Then for any large enough $C>0$, $\theta +C\omega $ is a Kähler form. Therefore, ( 21.13.29 ) follows. ( 21.13.30 ) is a direct consequence of ( 21.13.29 ). $\square$

The zero-divisor of $s$ on $U_{\sigma }$ is given by \[  \sum _{i=1}^ n \langle m, u_{\rho _ i} \rangle D_{\rho _ i},  \] see [ Proposition 4.1.2 , CLS11 ] . Therefore, \[  \nu _{Y_{\bullet }}(s)=\Bigl (\langle m, u_{\rho _1} \rangle ,\dots ,\langle m, u_{\rho _ n} \rangle \Bigr )=\Phi (m).  \] Conversely, every section of $L^ k$ is a finite linear combination of such characters. In the coordinates on $U_{\sigma }$ determined by $u_{\rho _1},\ldots ,u_{\rho _ n}$, the Okounkov valuation of a non-zero linear combination is the lexicographically first exponent among the characters with non-zero coefficient. Hence arbitrary sections give no valuations beyond the right-hand side of ( 21.13.34 ), and ( 21.13.34 ) follows. $\square$

title: Lemma 21.13.38
section: 21.13 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Lemma 21.13.38 . FCDBEF4DBD54 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ and assume that $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current. Then $\varphi $ admits a quasi-equisingular approximation $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ with the following additional properties: FE65BEEFF2E3 $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ and $\theta _{\varphi _ j}$ is a Kähler current for all $j\geq 1$; 5EC471277960 for each $j\geq 1$, there are $q_ j\in \mathbb Z_{>0}$ and toric eigen-sections \[  s_{j,1},\ldots ,s_{j,a_ j}\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^{q_ j})  \] such that \[  \varphi _ j=\frac{1}{q_ j}\log \sum _{\ell =1}^{a_ j}|s_{j,\ell }|_{h^{q_ j}}^2+\mathcal O(1).  \] Proof. Apply Demailly's Bergman-kernel approximation theorem [ Theorem 13.21 , Dem12 ] to the singular Hermitian metric $h\exp (-\varphi )$ on $L$. Since $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current, the theorem applies to the Hilbert spaces \[  \mathrm{H}^0\bigl (X,L^ q\otimes \mathcal I(q\varphi )\bigr )  \] for $q\gg 1$, endowed with the $L^2$-norm induced by $h^ q\exp (-q\varphi )$ and a fixed Kähler volume form. The usual decreasing extraction in Demailly's construction gives a quasi-equisingular approximation; taking $q$ sufficiently large at each step ensures that the approximants still have Kähler Chern currents. It remains to note that this construction is compatible with the torus action. Indeed, both $h$ and $\varphi $ are $T_ c$-invariant, hence the above Hilbert spaces and their $L^2$-inner products are $T_ c$-invariant. Since $T_ c$ is compact and abelian, each of these finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces admits an orthonormal basis consisting of toric eigen-sections. With such a basis, the corresponding Bergman potential has the displayed form and is $T_ c$-invariant. This proves the lemma. $\square$

title: Theorem 21.13.39
section: 21.13 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Theorem 21.13.39 . 8F3CCCDB83EC Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )_{>0}$. Then 3FD1A27C837D 21.13.40 \begin{equation}  \Phi _{\mathbb {R}}\Bigl ( \Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\Bigr )=\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\varphi ). \end{equation} In particular, 04CC3F6E758B 21.13.41 \begin{equation}  n!\operatorname{vol}\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )=\operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }. \end{equation} Proof. We first reduce to the case where $D|_{U_{\sigma }}=0$. In fact, changing $D$ to $D+\operatorname{div}\chi ^{m_{\sigma }}$ would result in changing $F_{\theta }$ to $F_{\theta }-m_{\sigma }$. Hence, $F_{\varphi }$ changes to $F_{\varphi }-m_{\sigma }$. Therefore, $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )$ becomes $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )-m_{\sigma }$. Taking ( 21.13.6 ) into consideration, we may assume that $m_{\sigma }=0$. Step 1 . We first reduce to the case where $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current. By 13.13.47 , we can find $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $\psi \leq \varphi $ and $\theta _{\psi }$ is a Kähler current. Taking the average along $T_ c$, we may assume that $\psi $ is $T_ c$-invariant. For each $t\in (0,1)$, we let \[  \varphi _ t=(1-t)\psi +t\varphi .  \] Suppose that Kähler current case is known. Then we get \[  \Phi _{\mathbb {R}}\Bigl ( \Delta (\theta ,\varphi _ t)\Bigr )=\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\varphi _ t)  \] for any $t\in (0,1)$. It follows from theorem 21.11.56 that \[  \Phi _{\mathbb {R}}\Bigl ( \Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\Bigr )\supseteq \Phi _{\mathbb {R}}\Bigl ( \Delta (\theta ,\varphi _ t)\Bigr )= \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\varphi _ t)  \] for any $t\in (0,1)$. Thanks to theorem 19.4.30 , we have \[  \Phi _{\mathbb {R}}\Bigl ( \Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\Bigr )\supseteq \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\varphi ).  \] Comparing the volumes of both sides using proposition 21.13.28 , ( 19.4.20 ), and the $\mathcal{I}$-goodness of toric singularities example 18.1.56 , we find that \[  n!\operatorname{vol}\Phi _{\mathbb {R}}\Bigl ( \Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\Bigr )=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n=\operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }=n!\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\varphi ).  \] In particular, we conclude ( 21.13.40 ). Step 2 . We handle the case where $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current. Let $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ be the quasi-equisingular approximation given by 21.13.38 . Now assume that the result is known for each $\varphi _ j$. Then \[  \Phi _{\mathbb {R}}\Bigl ( \Delta (\theta ,\varphi _ j)\Bigr )=\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\varphi _ j).  \] In particular, thanks to proposition 19.4.28 , \[  \Phi _{\mathbb {R}}\Bigl ( \Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\Bigr )\subseteq \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\varphi _ j)  \] for each $j\geq 1$. It follows from theorem 19.4.30 that \[  \Phi _{\mathbb {R}}\Bigl ( \Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\Bigr )\subseteq \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\varphi ).  \] Comparing the volumes of both sides using proposition 21.13.28 , ( 19.4.20 ), and example 18.1.56 , we conclude ( 21.13.40 ). Step 3 . It remains to prove the assertion for the analytic approximants appearing in Step 2. By 21.13.38 , these approximants may be chosen in the form \[  \varphi =\frac{1}{q}\log \sum _{i=1}^ a |s_ i|_{h^ q}^2+\mathcal O(1),  \] where $q\in \mathbb Z_{>0}$ and $s_1,\ldots ,s_ a\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ q)$ are toric eigen-sections. Let $m_1,\ldots ,m_ a\in qP_ D\cap M$ be the lattice points corresponding to $s_1,\ldots ,s_ a$. Observe that \[  \begin{aligned}  \Delta (\theta ,\varphi ) =& \overline{\nabla F_{\varphi }(N_{\mathbb {R}})}\\  =& \left\{  m\in M_{\mathbb {R}} : F_{\varphi }(n)-\langle m,n \rangle \textup{ is bounded from below} \right\} \\  =&  \left\{  m\in M_{\mathbb {R}}: q^{-1}\log \sum _{i=1}^ a \mathrm{e}^{\langle m_ i,n\rangle }-\langle m,n\rangle \textup{ is bounded below in } n \right\} \\  =&  q^{-1}\mathrm{Conv}\{ m_1,\ldots ,m_ a\} , \end{aligned}  \] where we have applied ( 21.13.23 ) on the second line and 21.11.62 on the third line. Since $m_1,\ldots ,m_ a\in qP_ D$, the preceding formula also shows that \[  \Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\subseteq P_ D.  \] Thus, if $m\in k\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\cap M$, then $m\in kP_ D\cap M$, and $\chi ^ m$ indeed determines a global section of $L^ k$. In particular, by the same separation argument as in 21.11.60 , for any $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$ and any $m\in k\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\cap M$, we have \[  |\chi ^ m|^2 \mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi }  \] is bounded from above on $T(\mathbb {C})$. In other words, the section $s$ of $L^ k$ corresponding to $m$ satisfies \[  s\in \mathrm{H}^0\left(X,L^ k\otimes \mathcal{I}_{\infty }(k\varphi )\right).  \] Therefore, \[  \nu _{Y_{\bullet }}(s)=\Phi (m)\in k\Delta _ k(\theta ,\varphi ),  \] where $\Delta _ k$ is defined in section 19.4 . Hence, \[  \Phi \Bigl (k\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\cap M\Bigr )\subseteq k\Delta _ k(\theta ,\varphi ).  \] Letting $k\to \infty $ and applying theorem 19.4.41 , we find that \[  \Phi _{\mathbb {R}}\Bigl (\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\Bigr ) \subseteq \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\varphi ).  \] Comparing the volumes of both sides using proposition 21.13.28 and ( 19.4.20 ), we conclude that the equality holds and ( 21.13.40 ) follows. $\square$

u (\varphi ,Y)>0$, then by corollary 21.13.43 , $\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )\cap Q_\sigma =\varnothing $. By convention the right-hand side of ( 21.13.80 ) is $0$, and the trace is not defined, so the left-hand side is $0$. Assume now that $

Corollary 21.13.81 . 9B7387A93262 The augmented base locus (with the reduced complex structure) of $D$ is a toric-invariant (possibly reducible) subvariety given by the union of the $V(	au )$'s, where $	au $ runs over the elements in $\Sigma $ such that \[  \dim Q_{	au }<n-\dim 	au {}^{\href{#sgpt-a0000106136}{6}}.  \] 6. ↩ Here we understand that $\dim \varnothing =-\infty $. Theorem 21.13.84 . 38F3E4DFCD04 Take $T$-invariant big divisors $D_1,\ldots ,D_ n$ on $X$. Consider $T_ c$-invariant closed positive $(1,1)$-currents $T_ i$ in $c_1(\mathcal{O}_ X(D_ i))$ for $i=1,\ldots ,n$. title: Theorem 21.13.53
section: 21.13 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Theorem 21.13.53 . 46AFD20390FF There are canonical bijections 4 between the following sets: B36269428F96 The set of $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$; BBC2A49C71B9 the set of $F\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P_ D)$, and 40A0E4A3390B the set of closed proper convex functions $G\in \mathrm{Conv}(M_{\mathbb {R}})$ satisfying \[  G|_{M_{\mathbb {R}}\setminus P_ D}\equiv \infty .  \] 4. ↩ In the earlier version of these constructions, I required additional conditions in 2 and 3 , namely $F\preceq F_{V_{\theta }}$ and $G\succeq G_{V_{\theta }}$ respectively. These conditions can be removed, since $G_{V_{\theta }}$ is always bounded, as suggested by Robert Berman. See theorem 21.13.45 . Proof. The proof is similar to that of theorem 21.12.13 , but due to its importance, we give the details. Again, the correspondence between 2 and 3 follows easily from proposition 21.11.38 . Given $\varphi $, we can construct $F_{\varphi }$ in 2 as explained earlier in ( 21.13.26 ). Conversely, suppose that $F\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P_ D)$, then $F\preceq F_{V_{\theta }}$ by theorem 21.13.45 . Then \[  \operatorname{Trop}^*\left(F-F_{\theta }\right)\in \mathrm{PSH}\left(T(\mathbb {C}),\theta |_{T(\mathbb {C})}\right)  \] by 21.12.7 . Since $F\preceq F_{V_{\theta }}$, we see that $\operatorname{Trop}^*(F-F_{\theta })$ is bounded from above. It follows that Grauert–Remmert's extension theorem theorem 5.14.10 is applicable, and this function extends to a unique $\theta $-psh function $\varphi $. The uniqueness of the extension guarantees that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$. The two maps are inverse to each other by construction. $\square$

text: Proposition 21.13.57 . BC781EB76285 Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ uniformly bounded from above. Then $\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ and \[  F_{\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i}=\bigvee _{i\in I}F_{\varphi _ i},\quad G_{\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i}=\operatorname{cl}\bigwedge _{i\in I} G_{\varphi _ i}.  \] Moreover, if $I$ is finite, then \[  G_{\bigvee _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}=\bigwedge _{i\in I} G_{\varphi _ i}.  \] Similarly, if $\{ \varphi _ i\} _{i\in I}$ is a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ such that $\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i\not\equiv -\infty $, then $\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ and \[  F_{\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}=\bigwedge _{i\in I}F_{\varphi _ i},\quad G_{\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}=\bigvee _{i\in I}G_{\varphi _ i}.  \]

title: Proposition 21.13.58
section: 21.13 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Proposition 21.13.58 . 0728D8B152D3 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$. Then $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ and D5353E18A697 21.13.59 \begin{equation}  G_{P_{\theta }[\varphi ]}(x)= \begin{cases}  G_{V_{\theta }}(x),& \textup{if } x\in \Delta (\theta ,\varphi );\\  \infty ,& \textup{otherwise}. \end{cases} \end{equation} Proof. By ( 16.3.7 ), \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]=\operatorname *{sup}_{C\in \mathbb {R}}{}\! {}^{*}\bigl ((\varphi +C)\land V_{\theta }\bigr ).  \] Hence $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ by proposition 21.13.55 , proposition 21.13.56 , proposition 21.13.57 . The same results give \[  G_{P_{\theta }[\varphi ]}=\operatorname{cl}\inf _{C\in \mathbb {R}}\left(G_{V_{\theta }}\lor (G_{\varphi }-C)\right).  \] Put \[  K=\inf _{C\in \mathbb {R}}\left(G_{V_{\theta }}\lor (G_{\varphi }-C)\right).  \] If $x\in \operatorname{Dom}G_{\varphi }$, then $G_{\varphi }(x)-C\leq G_{V_{\theta }}(x)$ for all large enough $C$, so $K(x)=G_{V_{\theta }}(x)$. If $x\notin \operatorname{Dom}G_{\varphi }$, then $K(x)=\infty $. By proposition 21.11.34 , we have $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )=\overline{\operatorname{Dom}G_{\varphi }}$. Moreover, theorem 21.13.45 gives $F_{V_{\theta }}\sim \operatorname{Supp}_{P_ D}$, hence $G_{V_{\theta }}\sim \chi _{P_ D}$ by Legendre duality. In particular, $G_{V_{\theta }}$ is finite and continuous on $P_ D$. Thus the lower semicontinuous regularization of $K$ is equal to $G_{V_{\theta }}$ on $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )$ and equal to $\infty $ outside $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )$. $\square$

title: Corollary 21.13.60
section: 21.13 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Corollary 21.13.60 . 396E3B9D09BD Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$. Then the following are equivalent: CD91E399605B $\varphi \preceq _ P \psi $; D043836BFE29 $\varphi \preceq _{\mathcal{I}} \psi $; 5F5AE307A1BE $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\subseteq \Delta (\theta ,\psi )$. Proof. 1 $\iff $ 2 . This follows from the $\mathcal{I}$-goodness of $\varphi $ and $\psi $, see example 18.1.56 . 1 $\iff $ 3 . When $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )_{>0}$, this follows from proposition 21.13.58 . In general, fix an ample toric-invariant divisor $H$ on $X$ and a toric-invariant Hermitian metric $h_ H$ on $\mathcal{O}_ X(H)$ such that $\omega _ H\coloneqq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ H$ is a Kähler form. We perturb $L$ to $L+m^{-1}H$ for $m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, then thanks to 21.11.47 , we find that \[  \Delta (\theta +m^{-1}\omega _ H,\varphi )\coloneqq m^{-1}\Delta (m\theta +\omega _ H,m\varphi )=\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )+m^{-1}\Delta \left(\mathcal{O}_ X(H)\right).  \] Then since $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta +m^{-1}\omega _ H)_{>0}$, we know that $\varphi \preceq _ P \psi $ if and only if \[  \Delta (\theta ,\varphi )+m^{-1}\Delta \left(\mathcal{O}_ X(H)\right)\subseteq \Delta (\theta ,\psi )+m^{-1}\Delta \left(\mathcal{O}_ X(H)\right)  \] for any $m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. The latter condition is equivalent to $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\subseteq \Delta (\theta ,\psi )$. $\square$

text: Corollary 21.13.61 . E1B465B480AB There is a canonical bijection \[  \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )/\sim _{P}=\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )/\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\rightarrow \left\{ K\in \mathcal{K}_ n: K \subseteq P_ D \right\} .  \] Here $\mathcal{K}_ n$ denotes the set of convex bodies in $\mathbb {R}^ n$, as in subsection 19.7.1 . Proof. Thanks to corollary 21.13.60 , we have the equality \[  \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )/\sim _{P}=\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )/\sim _{\mathcal{I}},  \] and the map \[  \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )/\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\rightarrow \left\{ K\in \mathcal{K}_ n: K \subseteq P_ D \right\}   \] is well-defined and injective. title: Proposition 21.13.62
section: 21.13 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Proposition 21.13.62 . D5C47A3AE82D Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$. There is a canonical bijection between the following sets: 7620AF887D78 The set of $T_ c$-invariant subgeodesics from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$; E254BA3D3052 the set of convex functions $F\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\times (0,1)\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ such that for each $r\in (0,1)$, the function F494EF2554FB 21.13.63 \begin{equation}  F_ r\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\rightarrow \mathbb {R},\quad n\mapsto F(n,r) \end{equation} satisfies $F_ r\to F_{\varphi _1}$ (resp. $F_ r\to F_{\varphi _0}$) everywhere as $r\to 1-$ (resp. $r\to 0+$). Proof. We begin with a subgeodesic $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Then we define $F\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\times (0,1)\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ as follows: \[  F(n,t)=F_{\varphi _ t}(n).  \] Define $F_ t$ as in ( 21.13.63 ), we have \[  \operatorname{Trop}^* F_ t-\operatorname{Trop}^* F_{\theta }=\varphi _ t,\quad t\in (0,1).  \] Let $t_ j\to 0+$. Since $\varphi _{t_ j}\to \varphi _0$ in $L^1$, after passing to a subsequence we have almost-everywhere convergence on $X$. Restricted to the open torus and using the tropical coordinates, this gives $F_{t_ j}\to F_{\varphi _0}$ almost everywhere on $N_{\mathbb R}$. Since the $F_{t_ j}$'s are convex and locally uniformly bounded above, theorem 21.11.20 upgrades this to pointwise convergence everywhere. As the limit is independent of the subsequence, $F_ t\to F_{\varphi _0}$ everywhere as $t\to 0+$. Similarly, $F_ t\to F_{\varphi _1}$ everywhere as $t\to 1-$. Next we show that $F$ is convex. Let $p_1\colon X\times S\rightarrow X$ be the projection, where \[  S\coloneqq \{ z\in \mathbb {C}: \mathrm{e}^{-1}<|z|^2<1\} .  \] Since $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ is a subgeodesic, its complexification $\Phi $ is $p_1^*\theta $-psh. Recall that $\Phi $ is defined as 71DDC2004810 21.13.64 \begin{equation}  \Phi (x,z)=\operatorname{Trop}^*\left( F_{-\log |z|^2}-F_{\theta } \right)(x). \end{equation} In particular, $\Psi \colon T(\mathbb {C})\times S\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ defined by \[  \Psi (x,z)\coloneqq \Phi (x,z)+\operatorname{Trop}^*F_{\theta }(x)=\operatorname{Trop}^*F_{-\log |z|^2}(x)  \] is plurisubharmonic and $T_ c\times S^1$-invariant. Fix a small enough $\epsilon >0$. We can find a decreasing sequence of $T_ c\times S^1$-invariant plurisubharmonic functions $\Psi _ i$ on $T(\mathbb {C})\times S_{\epsilon }$ converging to $\Psi $ everywhere, where \[  S_{\epsilon }\coloneqq \{ z\in \mathbb {C}: \mathrm{e}^{-1+\epsilon }<|z|^2<\mathrm{e}^{-\epsilon }\} .  \] Let us write \[  \Psi _ i(x,z)=\operatorname{Trop}^*F_{i,-\log |z|^2}(x)  \] for some $F_ i\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\times (\epsilon ,1-\epsilon )\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$. The same computation as in 21.12.7 shows that $F_ i$ is convex. It follows that $F$, as the decreasing limit of $F_ i$, is also convex on $N_{\mathbb {R}}\times (\epsilon ,1-\epsilon )$. Since $\epsilon >0$ is arbitrary, we conclude that $F$ is convex on $N_{\mathbb {R}}\times (0,1)$. Conversely, suppose that we are given $F$ in 2 . We define $\Phi \colon T(\mathbb {C})\times S\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ using ( 21.13.64 ). The arguments in the previous part can be reversed to show that $\Phi $ is $p_1^*\theta |_{T(\mathbb {C})\times S}$-psh. By our assumption, for each $t\in (0,1)$, we have 204454C17F1D 21.13.65 \begin{equation}  F_ t\leq tF_{\varphi _1}+(1-t)F_{\varphi _0}\leq F_{V_{\theta }}+C \end{equation} for some constant $C\in \mathbb {R}$ independent of the choice of $t$. Therefore, $\Phi $ is bounded from above and hence, by theorem 5.14.10 , admits a unique $p_1^*\theta $-psh extension to $X\times S$, which we still denote by $\Phi $. We let \[  \varphi _ t(x)=\Phi (x,\mathrm{e}^{-t/2})  \] for all $t\in (0,1)$ and $x\in X$. We claim that $(\varphi _ t)$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. For this purpose, we only need to show that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ has the correct boundary value. But from our assumption in 2 , we know that as $t\to 0+$ (resp. $t\to 1-$), $\varphi _ t\to \varphi _0$ (resp. $\varphi _ t\to \varphi _1$) almost everywhere. In particular, $\sup _ X \varphi _ t\geq -C'$ for some large constant $C'>0$ independent of $t\in (0,1)$. Therefore, together with ( 21.13.65 ), we deduce from proposition 5.17.3 that $\{ \varphi _ t\} _{t\in (0,1)}$ is a relatively compact family with respect to the $L^1$-topology. We need to show that each cluster point $\psi $ as $t\to 0+$ is equal to $\varphi _0$. But we already know that $\psi =\varphi _0$ almost everywhere. Hence we deduce $\psi =\varphi _0$ from proposition 5.14.6 . As $t\to 0+$, we have $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0$. Similarly, as $t\to 1-$, we have $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _1$. The two constructions are inverse to each other by construction. $\square$

text: Corollary 21.13.66 . 03A225BFC03C Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$. Then there is a canonical bijection between the following sets: 3A549D6065ED The set of $T_ c$-invariant subgeodesics from $\psi _0$ to $\psi _1$, where $\psi _0,\psi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ and $\psi _0\leq \varphi _0$, $\psi _1\leq \varphi _1$; C3D9271539D5 the set of closed proper convex functions $\Psi $ on $M_{\mathbb {R}}\times \mathbb {R}$ such that there is a closed proper convex function $G\in \mathrm{Conv}(M_{\mathbb {R}})$ satisfying D3A1BA3F5322 21.13.67 \begin{equation}  G(m)+(s\lor 0)\geq \Psi (m,s)\geq G_{\varphi _0}(m)\lor \left( G_{\varphi _1}(m)+s \right) \end{equation} for all $m\in M_{\mathbb {R}}$ and $s\in \mathbb {R}$. Proof. Let us begin with a subgeodesic $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ as in 1 . Let $F$ be the convex function as in proposition 21.13.62 . We extend $F$ to a function $F\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\times \mathbb {R}\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ as follows: For any $n\in N_{\mathbb {R}}$, we define \[  F(n,t)=\begin{cases}  F_{\psi _ t}(n),& \textup{if }0<t<1,\\  F_{\psi _0}(n),&  \textup{if }t=0,\\  F_{\psi _1}(n),& \textup{if }t=1,\\  \infty ,& \textup{if } t>1 \textup{ or }t<0. \end{cases}  \] Then $F$ is a proper closed convex function on $N_{\mathbb {R}}\times \mathbb {R}$. Let $\Psi $ be the Legendre transform of $F$. Then $\Psi $ is a proper closed convex function on $M_{\mathbb {R}}\times \mathbb {R}$ by theorem 21.11.24 . By ( 21.11.23 ), for any $m\in M_{\mathbb {R}}$ and $s\in \mathbb {R}$, we have \[  \begin{aligned}  \Psi (m,s)=& \sup _{n\in N_{\mathbb {R}},t\in [0,1]} \left( \langle m,n\rangle + ts-F(n,t)\right)\\  =&  \sup _{t\in [0,1]} \left( ts+F_ t^*(m) \right). \end{aligned}  \] Therefore, the latter half of ( 21.13.67 ) follows. Next recall that \[  \eta \coloneqq \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\psi _ t\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta ),  \] as follows from proposition 17.10.7 . Therefore, \[  \begin{aligned}  \Psi (m,s)=& \sup _{n\in N_{\mathbb {R}},t\in [0,1]} \left( \langle m,n\rangle + ts-F(n,t)\right)\\  \leq &  \sup _{n\in N_{\mathbb {R}},t\in [0,1]} \left( \langle m,n\rangle + ts-F_{\eta }(n)\right)\\  =&  \sup _{t\in [0,1]}ts+G_{\eta }(m)\\  =&  (s\lor 0)+G_{\eta }(m). \end{aligned}  \] Conversely, let us begin with a function $\Psi $ as in 2 . Let $F$ be the Legendre transform of $\Psi $. We first observe that $F(n,t)=\infty $ for all $n\in N_{\mathbb {R}}$ and $t\not\in [0,1]$. Indeed, the upper bound $\Psi \leq G+(s\lor 0)$ gives \[  F(n,t)\geq G^*(n)+\sup _{s\in \mathbb {R}}\left(ts-(s\lor 0)\right),  \] and the last supremum is infinite exactly when $t\notin [0,1]$. For $t\in [0,1]$, the lower bound $\Psi \geq G_{\varphi _0}\lor (G_{\varphi _1}+s)$ implies \[  \Psi (m,s)\geq (1-t)G_{\varphi _0}(m)+tG_{\varphi _1}(m)+ts.  \] Consequently, \[  F(n,t)\leq \left((1-t)G_{\varphi _0}+tG_{\varphi _1}\right)^*(n) \leq (1-t)F_{\varphi _0}(n)+tF_{\varphi _1}(n)  \] for all $t\in [0,1]$ and $n\in N_{\mathbb {R}}$. On the other hand, the upper bound $\Psi \leq G+(s\lor 0)$ gives \[  \begin{aligned}  F(n,t)=& \sup _{m\in M_{\mathbb {R}},s\in \mathbb {R}} \left(\langle m,n\rangle +ts-\Psi (m,s)\right)\\  \geq &  \sup _{m\in M_{\mathbb {R}},s\in \mathbb {R}} \left(\langle m,n\rangle +ts-G(m)-(s\lor 0)\right)\\  =&  G^*(n)+\sup _{s\in \mathbb {R}} \left( ts-(s\lor 0)\right)\\  =& \begin{cases}  G^*(n),& \text{if }t\in [0,1],\\  \infty ,& \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}\end{aligned}  \] The convexity of $F$ gives one-sided boundary limits \[  F_0(n)\coloneqq \lim _{t\to 0+}F(n,t),\quad F_1(n)\coloneqq \lim _{t\to 1-}F(n,t).  \] The estimates above give $F_0\leq F_{\varphi _0}$ and $F_1\leq F_{\varphi _1}$, and also show that $F_0,F_1\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P_ D)$. Let $\psi _0,\psi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ be the corresponding potentials given by theorem 21.13.53 . Then $\psi _0\leq \varphi _0$ and $\psi _1\leq \varphi _1$. Applying proposition 21.13.62 to the restriction of $F$ to $N_{\mathbb {R}}\times (0,1)$, we get a subgeodesic $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\psi _0$ to $\psi _1$. Thus $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ satisfies 1 . The two operations are inverse to each other by construction. $\square$

Since the geodesic is the upper envelope of toric subgeodesics, $\varphi _ t\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ for all $t\in (0,1)$. Therefore, by proposition 21.13.56 , \[  G_{\varphi _0}\lor G_{\varphi _1}=G_{\varphi _0\land \varphi _1}\not\equiv \infty .  \] In particular, ( 21.13.70 ) follows. Now by construction, \[  G_{\varphi _ t}(m)=\inf _{s\in \mathbb {R}} \left( \Psi '(m,s)-st\right)=(1-t)G_{\varphi _0}(m)+tG_{\varphi _1}(m)  \] for all $t\in (0,1)$. So ( 21.13.69 ) follows. $\square$

Therefore, we have a map from 2 to 1 . Conversely, given $\ell \in \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta ;\phi )$, it follows from corollary 21.13.68 that $G_{\ell _ t}$ is linear in $t\geq 0$ after restriction to $\operatorname{Int}\{ G_{\phi }<\infty \} $. Let \[  g'(m)= \begin{cases}  G_{\ell _1}(m)-G_{\phi }(m),&  m\in \operatorname{Int}\{ G_{\phi }<\infty \} ;\\  \infty ,&  m\in M_{\mathbb {R}}\setminus \operatorname{Int}\{ G_{\phi }<\infty \} . \end{cases}  \] Note that for $m\in \operatorname{Int}\{ G_{\phi }<\infty \} $, we actually have \[  g'(m)=\lim _{t\to \infty }t^{-1}G_{\ell _ t}(m).  \] Hence, $g'$ is a proper convex function on $M_{\mathbb {R}}$. It remains to argue that this map is the converse of the preceding map from 2 to 1 . The non-trivial point is to verify ( 21.13.72 ) holds for the $g$ we just constructed. Fix $t>0$. text: Corollary 21.13.81 . 9B7387A93262 The augmented base locus (with the reduced complex structure) of $D$ is a toric-invariant (possibly reducible) subvariety given by the union of the $V(\tau )$'s, where $\tau $ runs over the elements in $\Sigma $ such that \[  \dim Q_{\tau }<n-\dim \tau {}^{\href{#sgpt-a0000106136}{6}}.  \] 6. ↩ Here we understand that $\dim \varnothing =-\infty $. Proof. Apply corollary 21.13.79 to $\varphi =V_{\theta }$. Together with Nakamaye's theorem [ Theorem 5.7 , ELMNP09 ] and theorem 20.2.34 , this says that $V(\tau )$ lies in the augmented base locus exactly when the $\dim V(\tau )$-dimensional volume of $Q_{\tau }$ is zero, which is equivalent to $\dim Q_{\tau }<n-\dim \tau $. $\square$

title: Example 21.13.82
section: 21.13 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Example 21.13.82 . A14927C0973A Let us consider the example example 21.13.15 again, we consider the subvariety corresponding to $\sigma _7$. We have \[  Q_{\sigma _7}=\Bigl \{ m\in P_ D: \langle m,(1,1) \rangle =0 \Bigr \} .  \] The situation is explained in 21.13.83 . F8805F2A5BD0 21.13.83 The face $Q_{\sigma _7}=\{ m\in P_ D:\langle m,(1,1)\rangle =0\} $ is the single point $\{ (0,0)\} $, of dimension $0$ rather than the expected $1$. We find that $\dim Q_{\sigma _7}=0$, but the expected dimension is $2-1=1$. So the corresponding divisor, namely the exceptional divisor on $\mathrm{Bl}_0\mathbb {P}^2$ is in the non-Kähler locus. Similarly, we can verify that the non-Kähler locus consists only of this divisor.

title: Theorem 21.13.84
section: 21.13 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Theorem 21.13.84 . 38F3E4DFCD04 Take $T$-invariant big divisors $D_1,\ldots ,D_ n$ on $X$. Consider $T_ c$-invariant closed positive $(1,1)$-currents $T_ i$ in $c_1(\mathcal{O}_ X(D_ i))$ for $i=1,\ldots ,n$. Then 862A2BCBD614 21.13.85 \begin{equation}  n! \operatorname{vol}\Bigl ( \Delta (T_1),\ldots ,\Delta (T_ n) \Bigr )=\operatorname{vol}\left(T_1,\ldots ,T_ n \right). \end{equation} Proof. It suffices to prove the following assertion: 8E6671867292 21.13.86 \begin{equation}  \Delta (T_1+T_2)=\Delta (T_1)+\Delta (T_2).{}^{\href{#sgpt-a0000106283}{7}}\end{equation} In fact, assuming this, by induction, for each tuple of non-negative integers $C_1,\ldots ,C_ n$, we have \[  \Delta \left( \sum _{i=1}^ n C_ i T_ i \right)=\sum _{i=1}^ n C_ i \Delta (T_ i).  \] Comparing the volumes, we have \[  \operatorname{vol}\Delta \left( \sum _{i=1}^ n C_ i T_ i \right)=\sum _{i_1,\ldots ,i_ n=1}^ n C_{i_1}\cdots C_{i_ n} \operatorname{vol}\left(\Delta \left(T_{i_1}\right),\ldots ,\Delta \left(T_{i_ n}\right)\right).  \] On the other hand, by proposition 21.13.28 , the $\mathcal{I}$-goodness of toric singularities example 18.1.56 , and proposition 18.1.27 , we have \[  n! \operatorname{vol}\Delta \left( \sum _{i=1}^ n C_ i T_ i \right)=\operatorname{vol}\left( \sum _{i=1}^ n C_ i T_ i \right)=\sum _{i_1,\ldots ,i_ n=1}^ n C_{i_1}\cdots C_{i_ n} \operatorname{vol}\left(T_{i_1},\ldots ,T_{i_ n}\right).  \] Comparing the coefficients of the above two expressions, we conclude ( 21.13.85 ). It only remains to establish ( 21.13.86 ). For this purpose, we fix smooth $T_ c$-invariant Hermitian metrics $h_1$ and $h_2$ on $\mathcal{O}_ X(D_1)$ and $\mathcal{O}_ X(D_2)$ respectively. Correspondingly, take $h_1\otimes h_2$ as the reference Hermitian metric on $\mathcal{O}_ X(D_1+D_2)$. Write \[  \theta _1=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_1,\quad \theta _2=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_2.  \] We choose the rational section of $\mathcal O_ X(D_1+D_2)$ to be $s_{D_1}\otimes s_{D_2}$. With this choice and with the reference metric $h_1\otimes h_2$, the normalization ( 21.13.23 ) gives \[  F_{\theta _1+\theta _2}=F_{\theta _1}+F_{\theta _2}.  \] Thus \[  F_{\varphi _1+\varphi _2}=F_{\varphi _1}+F_{\varphi _2}.  \] Take $\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta _ i)$ with $T_ i=\theta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ i$ for $i=1,2$. Then $F_{\varphi _1}+F_{\varphi _2}$ is a candidate for $F_{\varphi _1+\varphi _2}$; see ( 21.13.26 ). Therefore, ( 21.13.86 ) follows from the equality of closed gradient images proved in 21.11.47 . $\square$ 7. ↩ This is slightly problematic when $n=1$, since $T_2$ is not defined stricto sensu . We take $D_2,T_2$ satisfying the same assumptions as $D_1,T_1$ in this case.

title: 22.1 Non-Archimedean pluripotential theory
text: This chapter develops a non-Archimedean pluripotential theory for compact Kähler manifolds. In the projective setting, Boucksom and Jonsson constructed a space of non-Archimedean psh metrics on the Berkovich analytification of a polarized variety. Our approach starts instead from the analytic objects developed in the previous chapters: $\mathcal I$-model test curves and their operations. The resulting theory agrees with the Boucksom–Jonsson theory in the projective case. The guiding idea is the Ross–Witt Nyström correspondence. A geodesic ray can be encoded by a test curve, and the $\mathcal I$-model version of this construction retains precisely the multiplier-ideal information relevant to algebraic approximation. For a pseudo-effective class $\{ \theta \} $, we define a non-Archimedean potential as an inverse system of $\mathcal I$-model test curves in the big classes $\{ \theta +\omega \} $, where $\omega $ ranges over Kähler forms. The transition maps are given by the $\mathcal I$-envelope. After the definition, we develop the basic operations on non-Archimedean potentials. Sums, translations, maxima, suprema, infima and rescalings are induced from the corresponding operations on test curves. We also define the non-Archimedean volume and prove its basic monotonicity and continuity properties. The next part of the chapter constructs the Duistermaat–Heckman measure of a non-Archimedean potential based on the theory of Okounkov bodies developed in section 19.1 . It is defined through Okounkov test curves and is shown to be independent of the chosen flag. The final part compares this construction with the Boucksom–Jonsson theory. In the projective case, we define the analytification of our non-Archimedean potentials and prove that the resulting space is naturally identified with the Boucksom–Jonsson space of psh non-Archimedean metrics. The present chapter is logically based on the test-curve formalism of section 17.11 , especially the $\mathcal I$-model theory of section 17.14 and the operations of section 17.15 . It is largely independent of section 21.13 , section 18.28 , while the comparison with Boucksom–Jonsson uses the non-Archimedean theory recalled in subsection 22.1.64 .

title: 22.1.1 The definition of non-Archimedean metrics
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$. Let $\textup{Käh}(X)$ be the set of Kähler forms on $X$ with the partial order given as follows: We say $\omega \preceq \omega '$ if $\omega \geq \omega '$. Note that the partially ordered set $\textup{Käh}(X)$ is a directed set. Let $\theta $ be a closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form representing a pseudo-effective cohomology class. Definition 22.1.2 . 657951EB240B We define \[  \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )=\varprojlim _{\omega \in \textup{Käh}(X)} \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta +\omega )_{>0}{}^{\href{#sgpt-a0000106603}{1}} \] in the category of sets, where the transition maps are given as follows: Suppose that $\omega ,\omega '\in \textup{Käh}$ and $\omega \geq \omega '$. Then the transition map is defined in proposition 17.14.6 : A99876729E5F 22.1.3 \begin{equation}  P_{\theta +\omega }[\bullet ]_{\mathcal{I}}\colon \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta +\omega ')_{>0}\rightarrow \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta +\omega )_{>0}. \end{equation} Note that the transition maps are compatible: \[  P_{\theta +\omega ''}[P_{\theta +\omega '}[\varphi ]_\mathcal {I}]_\mathcal {I}=P_{\theta +\omega ''}[\varphi ]_\mathcal {I},\quad \forall \,  \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta +\omega )_{>0}  \] for $\omega \leq \omega '\leq \omega ''$, since both sides are $\mathcal{I}$-model and are $\mathcal{I}$-equivalent to $\varphi $. 1. ↩ The cumbersome projective limit can be avoided if instead of relying on the language of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions, we use that of augmented nef b-divisors developed in definition 20.1.32 instead. But given the fact that these two formulations are completely equivalent to each other by corollary 20.1.34 , we just stick to the slightly more traditional language here. Recall that $\mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ is defined in definition 17.14.1 . In general, when we denote an element in $\mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )$ by $\Gamma $, its component in $\mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta +\omega )_{>0}$ ($\omega \in \textup{Käh}(X)$) will be written either as $\Gamma ^{\theta +\omega }$ or as $P_{\theta +\omega }[\Gamma ]_{\mathcal{I}}$. Note that $\Gamma ^{\theta +\omega }_{\max }$ is independent of the choice of $\omega \in \textup{Käh}(X)$. We denote this common value by $\Gamma _{\max }$. Remark 22.1.4 . C864B821AD8B Thanks to proposition 17.14.3 , for any other $\theta '$ representing $\{ \theta \} $, we have a canonical bijection \[  \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )\xrightarrow {\sim }\mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta ').  \] Moreover, these bijections satisfy the cocycle condition. If we view the set of closed real smooth $(1,1)$-forms representing $\{ \theta \} $ as a category with a unique morphism between any two objects, then we can define \[  \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\{ \theta \} )=\varprojlim _{\theta } \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta ).  \] This definition is independent of the choice of the explicit representative of the cohomology class $\{ \theta \} $. However, given the fact that our notation is already quite heavy, we stick to the set $\mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )$. The constructions below are independent of the choice of $\theta $ within its cohomology class. Proposition 22.1.5 . B80F3474DB2F Let $\Gamma \in \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )$. Then given $\omega ,\omega '\in \textup{Käh}(X)$ with $\omega \geq \omega '$, we have \[  P_{\theta +\omega }\left[ \Gamma ^{\theta +\omega '}_{-\infty } \right]=P_{\theta +\omega }\left[ \Gamma ^{\theta +\omega '}_{-\infty } \right]_{\mathcal{I}} = \Gamma ^{\theta +\omega }_{-\infty }.  \] Proof. Since for any $\tau <\Gamma _{\max }$, the potential $\Gamma ^{\theta +\omega '}_{\tau }$ is $\mathcal{I}$-good by example 18.1.11 , it follows that \[  P_{\theta +\omega }\left[ \Gamma ^{\theta +\omega '}_{\tau } \right]=P_{\theta +\omega }\left[ \Gamma ^{\theta +\omega '}_{\tau } \right]_{\mathcal{I}}=\Gamma ^{\theta +\omega }_{\tau }  \] for all $\tau <\Gamma _{\max }$. Our assertion follows from proposition 16.4.9 and proposition 16.6.30 . $\square$ Proposition 22.1.6 . 2CB4FA8703B1 There is a natural injective map \[  \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )_{>0}\hookrightarrow \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta ),\quad \Gamma \mapsto \left(P_{\theta +\omega }[\Gamma ]_{\mathcal{I}}\right)_{\omega \in \textup{Käh}(X)}.  \] In the sequel, we do not distinguish an element of $\mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ from its image in $\mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )$. Note that given $\Gamma \in \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )_{>0}$, the value of $\Gamma _{\max }$ does not depend on whether we view it as an element of $\mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ or of $\mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )$. Proof. The map is well-defined by the compatibility of the transition maps. It suffices to argue its injectivity. Suppose that $\Gamma ,\Gamma '\in \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ and \[  P_{\theta +\omega }[\Gamma ]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta +\omega }[\Gamma ']_{\mathcal{I}}  \] for some Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. Then $\Gamma _{\max }=\Gamma '_{\max }$ and for any $\tau <\Gamma _{\max }$, we have \[  \Gamma _{\tau }\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\Gamma '_{\tau }  \] by proposition 16.8.17 . It follows again from proposition 16.8.17 that \[  \Gamma _{\tau }=\Gamma '_{\tau }.  \] This completes the proof. $\square$ Definition 22.1.7 . A92D6DFAC0CF Let $\Gamma \in \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )$. We define its volume as follows: \[  \operatorname{vol}\Gamma \coloneqq \lim _{\omega \in \textup{Käh}(X)} \int _ X \left(\theta +\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +\omega }_{-\infty }\right)^ n\in [0,\infty ).  \] Observe that the net is decreasing, so the limit exists. Proposition 22.1.8 . 47A4DA9EBA71 Let $\Gamma \in \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )_{>0}$. Then \[  \operatorname{vol}\Gamma =\int _ X \left(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma _{-\infty }\right)^ n.  \] Proof. This follows from proposition 16.4.4 , corollary 16.4.8 and proposition 17.12.19 . $\square$ Lemma 22.1.9 . 587EEDE88F4F Let $\Gamma \in \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )$, let $\omega $ be a Kähler form on $X$, and let $0<t\leq 1$. Then for every $\tau <\Gamma _{\max }$, we have \[  \begin{aligned} & \int _ X \left(\theta +t\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +t\omega }_{-\infty }\right)^ n-\int _ X \left(\theta +t\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +t\omega }_{\tau }\right)^ n\\  \leq {}& \int _ X \left(\theta +\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +\omega }_{-\infty }\right)^ n-\int _ X \left(\theta +\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +\omega }_{\tau }\right)^ n. \end{aligned}  \] Proof. For $\sigma \in \{ -\infty ,\tau \} $, put \[  S_ t^\sigma =\theta +t\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +t\omega }_{\sigma }.  \] By the transition compatibility and proposition 22.1.5 , example 18.1.11 , proposition 16.3.10 , projecting $\Gamma ^{\theta +t\omega }_{\sigma }$ to the class $\theta +\omega $ does not change the total mass computed in the larger class. Thus \[  \int _ X \left(\theta +\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +\omega }_{\sigma }\right)^ n = \int _ X \left(S_ t^\sigma +(1-t)\omega \right)^ n.  \] Expanding the right-hand side and subtracting the two identities for $\sigma =-\infty $ and $\sigma =\tau $, we get \[  \begin{aligned} & \int _ X \left(\theta +\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +\omega }_{-\infty }\right)^ n-\int _ X \left(\theta +\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +\omega }_{\tau }\right)^ n\\  ={}& \sum _{a=0}^ n \binom {n}{a}(1-t)^{n-a} \left(\int _ X (S_ t^{-\infty })^ a\wedge \omega ^{n-a}-\int _ X (S_ t^\tau )^ a\wedge \omega ^{n-a}\right). \end{aligned}  \] Since $\Gamma ^{\theta +t\omega }_{-\infty }\geq \Gamma ^{\theta +t\omega }_{\tau }$, each summand is non-negative by the monotonicity theorem for mixed non-pluripolar products. Keeping only the term $a=n$ gives the desired inequality. $\square$ Lemma 22.1.10 . 9A2678C2C223 The image of the canonical injection \[  \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )_{>0}\hookrightarrow \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )  \] is given by the set of $\Gamma \in \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )$ with positive volume. Proof. By proposition 22.1.8 , every element in the image has positive volume. Conversely, take $\Gamma \in \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )$ with positive volume. We want to construct $\Gamma '\in \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ representing $\Gamma $. Fix a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. Define 717C364BF812 22.1.11 \begin{equation}  \Gamma '_{\tau }\coloneqq \lim _{k\to \infty }\Gamma ^{\theta +k^{-1}\omega }_{\tau },\quad \tau <\Gamma _{\max }. \end{equation} We claim that it suffices to show 80067294986D 22.1.12 \begin{equation}  \varliminf _{k\to \infty }\int _ X \left(\theta +k^{-1}\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +k^{-1}\omega }_{\tau }\right)^ n>0 \end{equation} for some $\tau <\Gamma _{\max }$. If this holds, then the argument of 17.12.6 implies that the same holds for all $\tau <\Gamma _{\max }$. Then proposition 16.4.4 , proposition 16.6.29 guarantee that $\Gamma '\in \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ and represents $\Gamma $. It remains to argue ( 22.1.12 ). Let $\epsilon =\operatorname{vol}\Gamma >0$. Take $\tau <\Gamma _{\max }$ so that \[  \int _ X \left(\theta +\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +\omega }_{-\infty }\right)^ n-\int _ X \left(\theta +\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +\omega }_{\tau }\right)^ n<\epsilon /2.  \] Therefore, by 22.1.9 , for any $k\geq 1$, \[  \int _ X \left(\theta +k^{-1}\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +k^{-1}\omega }_{-\infty }\right)^ n-\int _ X \left(\theta +k^{-1}\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +k^{-1}\omega }_{\tau }\right)^ n<\epsilon /2.  \] By the definition of $\operatorname{vol}\Gamma $, the first integral in the preceding line tends to $\epsilon $ as $k\to \infty $. Hence \[  \varliminf _{k\to \infty }\int _ X \left(\theta +k^{-1}\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma ^{\theta +k^{-1}\omega }_{\tau }\right)^ n\geq \epsilon /2>0,  \] which proves ( 22.1.12 ). $\square$ Example 22.1.13 . 796F447D96B6 Fix $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. We can define an associated non-Archimedean metric \[  \Gamma ^{\varphi }\in \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )  \] as follows: FB0E6FB2D0F7 $\Gamma ^{\varphi }_{\max }=0$; 7A4B948C1C94 for any $\omega \in \textup{Käh}(X)$ and any $\tau <0$, we set \[  \Gamma ^{\varphi ,\theta +\omega }_{\tau }=P_{\theta +\omega }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Such non-Archimedean metrics are called homogeneous non-Archimedean metrics. Observe that \[  \operatorname{vol}\Gamma ^{\varphi }=\operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }.  \] See proposition 18.1.27 and the footnote there. Definition 22.1.14 . CCAAC9DA4E2F Let $\omega $ be a closed real smooth positive $(1,1)$-form on $X$. We define the map \[  P_{\theta +\omega }[\bullet ]_{\mathcal{I}}\colon \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )\rightarrow \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta +\omega )  \] as follows: Given $\Gamma \in \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )$, we define $P_{\theta +\omega }[\Gamma ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ as the element such that for any $\omega '\in \textup{Käh}(X)$, we have \[  P_{\theta +\omega }[\Gamma ]_{\mathcal{I}}^{\theta +\omega +\omega '}=\Gamma ^{\theta +\omega +\omega '}.  \] It is straightforward to check that under the identification of proposition 22.1.6 , the map $P_{\theta +\omega }[\bullet ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ extends the map ( 22.1.3 ). Proposition 22.1.15 . 3943AA7119C5 The maps $P_{\theta +\omega }[\bullet ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ in definition 22.1.14 together induce a bijection 29D3530031C6 22.1.16 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )\xrightarrow {\sim } \varprojlim _{\omega \in \textup{Käh}(X)}\mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta +\omega ). \end{equation} Proof. It is a tautology that the maps $P_{\theta +\omega }[\bullet ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ in definition 22.1.14 are compatible with the transition maps. So the map ( 22.1.16 ) is well-defined. It is injective by the same argument as proposition 22.1.6 . We argue the surjectivity. By unfolding the definitions, an object in the target of ( 22.1.16 ) is an assignment: With each $\omega \in \textup{Käh}(X)$, we associate a family $(\Gamma ^{\omega ,\omega '})_{\omega '\in \textup{Käh}(X)}$ satisfying: 5067A37E976E $\Gamma ^{\omega ,\omega '}\in \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta +\omega +\omega ')_{>0}$ for each $\omega ,\omega '\in \textup{Käh}(X)$; CDB9ED278B54 for each $\omega ,\omega ',\omega ''\in \textup{Käh}(X)$ satisfying $\omega ''\geq \omega '$, we have \[  P_{\theta +\omega +\omega ''}\left[\Gamma ^{\omega ,\omega '}\right]_{\mathcal{I}}=\Gamma ^{\omega ,\omega ''};  \] 3EBB3E3A9CF6 for each $\omega ,\omega ',\omega ''\in \textup{Käh}(X)$ satisfying $\omega \leq \omega '$, we have \[  P_{\theta +\omega '+\omega ''}\left[\Gamma ^{\omega ,\omega ''}\right]_{\mathcal{I}}=\Gamma ^{\omega ',\omega ''}.  \] The preimage of such an object is given by the family $(\Gamma ^{\theta +\omega })_{\omega \in \textup{Käh}(X)}$ given by \[  \Gamma ^{\theta +\omega }=\Gamma ^{\omega /2,\omega /2}.  \] The fact that the image of $\Gamma $ is as expected follows directly from the definitions. $\square$ With an almost identical argument involving proposition 16.4.4 , we get Proposition 22.1.17 . 817C1BB3E570 The maps $P_{\theta +\omega }[\bullet ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ in definition 22.1.14 and the injective maps proposition 22.1.6 together induce bijections 258B0F2A2F95 22.1.18 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )\xrightarrow {\sim } \varprojlim _{\omega }\mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta +\omega )_{>0}\xrightarrow {\sim } \varprojlim _{\omega }\mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta +\omega ), \end{equation} where $\omega $ runs over either the partially ordered set of all smooth closed real positive $(1,1)$-forms with positive volume 2 on $X$ or $\textup{Käh}(X)$. 2. ↩ This partially ordered set is not directed. Corollary 22.1.19 . 347399E47277 Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a compact Kähler manifold $Y$. Then $\pi ^*$ induces a bijection \[  \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(X,\theta )\xrightarrow {\sim } \mathrm{PSH}^{\mathrm{NA}}(Y,\pi ^*\theta ).  \] Proof. This follows immediately from proposition 22.1.17 . $\square$ It is immediate to verify that $\pi ^*$ in corollary 22.1.19 extends the map proposition 17.14.4 .
