title: Definition 21.11.15
text: Definition 21.11.15 . 61B746F5E884 Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$. The closure $\operatorname{cl}F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ of $F$ is defined as follows: If $F(n)=-\infty $ for some $n\in N$, then $\operatorname{cl}F\coloneqq -\infty $. Otherwise, we define $\operatorname{cl}F$ as the lower semicontinuity regularization of $F$. A convex function $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ is closed if $F=\operatorname{cl}F$. In other words, $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ is closed if one of the following conditions holds: 9B2264291DE3 $F\equiv -\infty $; 55523AC55CA5 $F\equiv \infty $; C1225E82131E $F$ is proper and lower semicontinuous.

title: Proposition 21.11.16
text:
Proposition 21.11.16 . E013E1966E44 Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ be a closed convex function. Then $F$ is the supremum of all affine functions lying below $F$. Proof. For a closed proper $F$, finite-dimensional Fenchel duality gives
\[F(x)=F^{**}(x)=\sup_p\{\langle p,x\rangle-F^*(p)\}.\]
For every $p$ with $F^*(p)<+\infty$, the expression in braces is an affine minorant of $F$, by the definition of conjugacy. Conversely, every affine minorant $\langle p,x\rangle+c$ satisfies $c\leq-F^*(p)$. Thus the supremum is exactly that of all affine minorants. If $F\equiv+\infty$, arbitrary constant minorants already have supremum $+\infty$. If $F\equiv-\infty$, there are no finite affine minorants and their supremum is $-\infty$.

title: Theorem 21.11.17
text: Theorem 21.11.17 . 7E0B71CF3B0E Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then $\operatorname{cl}F$ is a closed proper convex function. Moreover, $\operatorname{cl}F$ agrees with $F$ except possibly on the relative boundary of $\operatorname{Dom}F$. Proof. Apply the closure theorem for proper convex functions . It proves that the lower semicontinuous regularization of $F$ is closed and proper and agrees with $F$ on the relative interior of its effective domain. Since $F$ is proper, this regularization is exactly the closure defined here. Outside the closure of $\operatorname{Dom}F$, both functions are $+\infty$: a neighborhood misses the effective domain, so the lower semicontinuous regularization is $+\infty$ there. Every remaining point outside the relative boundary belongs to the relative interior of the domain. Therefore disagreement is possible only on that relative boundary, as asserted.

title: Proposition 21.11.18
text: Proposition 21.11.18 . B6B15657CD64 Let $F,F'\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ be closed convex functions. Assume that A4BAF58116DC $\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F=\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F'$, and FAD3EA2C74FA $F=F'$ on $\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F$. Then $F=F'$. Proof. For proper closed functions this is the uniqueness assertion in the convex closure theorem . More explicitly, the closure of the epigraph over the relative interior of the effective domain is the whole epigraph: for a point of the epigraph, take convex combinations with a fixed epigraph point whose base is in that relative interior, and let the coefficient of the fixed point tend to zero. Thus identical values on the common relative interior give identical epigraphs and hence identical functions. The improper cases in the definition of closedness are also determined: empty effective domain means the function identically $+\infty$; if one function is identically $-\infty$, the common relative interior is $N$ and the value agreement makes the other identical to it. These cases complete the proof.

title: Definition 21.11.19
text: Definition 21.11.19 . CC63E6A637E8 Given $F,F'\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$, we write $F\preceq F'$ if there is $C\in \mathbb {R}$ such that \[  F\leq F'+C.  \] We say $F\sim F'$ if $F\preceq F'$ and $F'\preceq F$ both hold.

title: Theorem 21.11.20
text: Theorem 21.11.20 . A7E9B5A114CA Let $C\subseteq N$ be an open subset. Let $(f_ i)_{i>0}$ be a sequence of real-valued convex functions on $C$. Suppose that the sequence converges on a dense subset of $C$ and the limit is finite. Then the limit \[  f(x)\coloneqq \lim _{i\to \infty } f_ i(x)  \] exists for all $x\in C$ and is convex on $C$. Moreover, the sequence $(f_ i)_ i$ converges uniformly to $f$ on each compact subset of $C$. Proof. On every open convex ball relatively compact in $C$, dense convergence for finite convex functions applies to the restriction of the given dense set and supplies a finite convex local limit with locally uniform convergence. Local limits agree on overlaps, because they are pointwise limits of the same sequence. They therefore define a finite function $f$ on $C$. Every compact subset of $C$ is covered by finitely many smaller such balls. Taking the maximum of the finitely many uniform error bounds proves uniform convergence on that compact set. Passing to the limit in each convexity inequality proves convexity wherever the corresponding segment lies in $C$; in the usual convention that the domain of a convex function is convex, this is convexity on $C$. In particular the limiting values at the original dense set determine $f$ uniquely.

title: 21.11.21 Legendre transform
text:
Let $N$ be a real vector space of finite dimension and $M$ be the dual vector space. The pairing $M	imes Nightarrow \mathbb {R}$ will be denoted by $\langle  ullet ,  ullet angle $. Definition 21.11.22 . 2E5E29E9A58B Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ be a convex function. We define the Legendre transform of $F$ as the function $F^*\in \mathrm{Conv}(M)$: E1AD8A1437E2 21.11.23  egin{equation}  F^*(m)\coloneqq \sup _{n\in N} \left( \langle m,n angle -F(n) ight)=\sup _{n\in \operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F} \left( \langle m,n angle -F(n) ight). \end{equation} The latter equality follows from [ Corollary 12.2.2 , Roc70 ] . 


Recall the well-known Legendre–Fenchel duality [ Theorem 12.2 , Roc70 ] . Theorem 21.11.24 . 258227E5D497 Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$. Then $F^*$ is a closed convex function. The function $F^*$ is proper if and only if $F$ is. Moreover, we have $(\operatorname{cl}F)^*=F^*$ and \[  F^{**}=\operatorname{cl}F.  \] Proof. For proper $F$, all assertions are the finite-dimensional Fenchel theorem , whose separation proof is given earlier: $F^*$ is closed and proper, $(\operatorname{cl}F)^*=F^*$, and $F^{**}=\operatorname{cl}F$. For completeness consider improper convex functions. If $F\equiv+\infty$, then $F^*\equiv-\infty$ and $F^{**}\equiv+\infty$. Otherwise an improper $F$ takes $-\infty$ somewhere, so every $F^*(p)$ is $+\infty$, its biconjugate is identically $-\infty$, and this is exactly the closure prescribed in the definition. Its conjugate is again identically $+\infty$. Neither conjugate is proper in these improper cases. This proves the equivalence of properness and all the identities also at the extended-valued extremes. Example 21.11.25 . 1A7C0B007516 Let $P\subseteq M$ be a closed convex subset. Then \[  \operatorname{Supp}_ P^*=\chi _ P,\quad \chi _ P^*=\operatorname{Supp}_ P.  \] See [ Theorem 13.2 , Roc70 ] . The following special case will be useful to us in the sequel. Corollary 21.11.26 . 8C4DFDD0ADE0 Let $F\colon (0,\infty )ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a convex function. If we define $G\colon \mathbb {R}ightarrow (-\infty ,\infty ]$ by \[  G(	au )=\sup _{t>0} \Bigl ( t	au -F(t) \Bigr ),  \] then $G$ is a convex function and E918B6149A40 21.11.27  egin{equation}  F(t)=G^*(t),\quad  orall t>0. \end{equation} Moreover, 3B0DC2BF53F0 21.11.28  egin{equation}  G(	au )=\sup _{t\in \mathbb {R}_{>0}} \Bigl ( t	au -F(t) \Bigr )=\sup _{t\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}} \Bigl ( t	au -F(t) \Bigr ). \end{equation} Proof. We distinguish two cases. First suppose that $F(t)=-\infty $ for some $t>0$. Then $F(t)=-\infty $ for all $t>0$ by the convexity of $F$. Our assertions are clear in this case. Next assume that $F(t)
eq -\infty $ for all $t>0$. In this case, theorem 21.11.17 guarantees that $F$ admits a closed proper extension $	ilde{F}\in \mathrm{Conv}(\mathbb {R})$ with \[  	ilde{F}(t)=\infty ,\quad  orall t<0.  \] It follows from ( 21.11.23 ) that \[  G(	au )=	ilde{F}^*(	au ),\quad  orall 	au \in \mathbb {R}.  \] Now theorem 21.11.24 implies ( 21.11.27 ). Finally ( 21.11.28 ) follows from the continuity of $F$. $\square$ Proposition 21.11.29 . C3CC440747D6 Let $F\colon Nightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$. Define $F^*\colon Mightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ by \[  F^*(m)\coloneqq \sup _{n\in N} \left( \langle m,n angle -F(n) ight).  \] Then \[  F^*=(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{CE}F)^*.  \] Proof. Put $H=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{CE}F$. Since $H\leq F$, order reversal gives $H^*\geq F^*$. Fix $p$ with $F^*(p)$ finite. The affine function $\ell(x)=\langle p,xangle-F^*(p)$ lies below $F$, hence below its convex envelope and below its lower semicontinuous regularization, because $\ell$ itself is continuous. Thus $\langle p,xangle-H(x)\leq F^*(p)$ for all $x$, proving $H^*(p)\leq F^*(p)$. If $F^*(p)=+\infty$, the reverse inequality already gives equality. If $F^*(p)=-\infty$, then $F$ is identically $+\infty$; its closed convex envelope is also identically $+\infty$, and the equality is immediate. This treats every possible value of the conjugate. See [ Corollary 12.1.1 , Roc70 ] . Definition 21.11.30 . D6A0CB1B8846 Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ and $n\in N$. An element $m\in M$ is a subgradient (in the sense of Alexandrov) of $F$ at $n$ if F6F028287E9D 21.11.31  egin{equation}  F(n')\geq F(n)+\langle n'-n,m angle ,\quad  orall n'\in N. \end{equation} The set of subgradients of $F$ at $n$ is denoted by $
abla F(n)$. More generally, for any subset $E\subseteq N$, we write \[  
abla F(E)= igcup _{n\in E}
abla F(n).  \] Definition 21.11.32 . 08E83421373C Given $F,F'\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$, we write $F\preceq _ P F'$ if \[  \overline{
abla F(N)}\subseteq \overline{
abla F'(N)}.  \] We write $F\sim _ P F'$ if $F\preceq _ P F'$ and $F'\preceq _ P F$. Theorem 21.11.33 . A57F525B7ABC Suppose that $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then the following hold: 8BEAD5D03F60 For any $n
ot\in \operatorname{Dom}F$, $

abla F(n)
eq \varnothing $; moreover, for any $n'\in N$, we have \[  \partial _{n'} F(n)=\sup \left\{ \langle n', m angle : m\in 
abla F(n)ight\} ;  \] 891D0FE828BD for $n\in N$, the set $
abla F(n)$ is non-empty and bounded if and only if $n\in \operatorname{Int}\operatorname{Dom}F$. Proof. Subgradients at points outside the effective domain are empty by definition. On the relative interior, existence and the directional formula follow from local convex regularity applied in the affine span $A$ of the domain. To view a subgradient as a functional on $N$, extend its restriction to the direction space of $A$ by a linear functional. Any functional vanishing on that direction space may be added without changing the subgradient inequality. Thus for a direction outside that space the supremum in the directional formula is $+\infty$, just as the one-sided directional derivative is; for tangent directions it is the relative formula. At an interior point of the domain, local Lipschitz continuity bounds all subgradients: if $|F(x+v)-F(x)|\leq L|v|$ for small $v$, the subgradient inequality for $v$ and $-v$ gives $|\langle p,vangle|\leq L|v|$, hence $|p|\leq L$. Conversely, suppose the subgradient set is nonempty at a point $x$ of the domain which is not interior. A supporting hyperplane to the closure of the convex domain at $x$ supplies a nonzero $q$ with $\langle q,y-xangle\leq0$ for every $y$ in the domain. If $p$ is a subgradient, then so is $p+tq$ for every $t\geq0$, so the set is unbounded. Supporting hyperplanes also exist when the domain lies in a proper affine subspace, by taking an annihilating functional. This proves the final equivalence. For the proof, we refer to [ Theorem 23.4 , Roc70 ] . Proposition 21.11.34 . 8B18F2B2DE3B Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then \[  
abla F(N)\subseteq \operatorname{Dom}F^*.  \] If moreover $F$ is closed, we have C0D69D19C109 21.11.35  egin{equation}  \operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F^*\subseteq 
abla F(N). \end{equation} In particular, if $F$ is a proper closed convex function on $N$, then \[  \overline{
abla F(N)}=\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F^*}.  \] Proof. If $p\in\partial F(x)$, the subgradient inequality gives $F^*(p)=\langle p,xangle-F(x)<+\infty$, proving the first inclusion. Now assume $F$ is closed and let $p$ lie in the relative interior of $\operatorname{Dom}F^*$. The conjugate is closed and proper by Fenchel duality , so it has a subgradient $x$ at $p$. The same duality theorem gives $p\in\partial F(x)$. Thus the relative interior is contained in the subgradient image. Taking closures in the two inclusions and using that a nonempty convex set has the same closure as its relative interior proves the equality of closures. Proof. Suppose that $m\in 
abla F(n)$ for some $n\in N$. Then ( 21.11.31 ) holds. In particular, \[  \langle m,n'angle -F(n')\leq \langle m,nangle -F(n).  \] It follows that \[  F^*(m)\leq \langle m,nangle -F(n)<\infty .  \] ( 21.11.35 ) is proved in [ Corollary 23.5.1 , Roc70 ] . For the last assertion, it suffices to observe that $\overline{\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F^*}=\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F^*}$. $\square$ Proposition 21.11.36 . 7A76E56311F5 Let $\{ F_ i\} _{i\in I}$ be a non-empty family in $\mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then \[  \left( igwedge _{i\in I} F_ iight)^*= igvee _{i\in I} F_ i^*,\quad \left( igvee _{i\in I} \operatorname{cl}F_ iight)^*=\operatorname{cl} igwedge _{i\in I} F_ i^*.  \] If $I$ is finite and $\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F_ i}$ is independent of the choice of $i\in I$, then \[  \left( igvee _{i\in I} F_ iight)^*= igwedge _{i\in I} F_ i^*.  \] Recall that $\wedge $ is defined in definition 21.11.10 and $\lor $ in definition 21.11.11 . See [ Theorem 16.5 , Roc70 ] for the proof. Proposition 21.11.37 . 36CA6A68994E Let $F_1,\ldots ,F_ r\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$ ($r\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$). Assume that \[   igcap _{i=1}^ r\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}(F_ i)
eq \varnothing ,  \] then for any $m\in M$, \[  \left( \sum _{i=1}^ r F_ i ight)^*(m)=\inf \left\{ \sum _{i=1}^ r F_ i^*(m_ i):m_1,\ldots ,m_ r\in M, \sum _{i=1}^ r m_ i=m ight\} .  \] Proof. For every decomposition $p=\sum_i p_i$, the defining inequalities for the conjugates give $(\sum_iF_i)^*(p)\leq\sum_iF_i^*(p_i)$. It remains to prove the reverse inequality when the left side is finite. The case $r=1$ is immediate. For $r\geq2$, put
\[V(z_1,\ldots,z_{r-1})=\inf_x\left\{\sum_{i<r}F_i(x+z_i)+F_r(x)-\langle p,xangleight\}.\]
This is convex, being an infimum over the fibers of a convex epigraph. Its value at zero is $-(\sum_iF_i)^*(p)$, which is finite. Choose $x_0$ in the common relative interior in the hypothesis. The product of the effective domains has $(x_0,\ldots,x_0)$ in its relative interior. The linear map $(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\mapsto(x_1-x_r,\ldots,x_{r-1}-x_r)$ maps a relative neighborhood of this point onto a relative neighborhood of zero in its image affine span: a surjective linear map between finite-dimensional spaces has a continuous linear right inverse. Consequently zero lies in the relative interior of $\operatorname{Dom}V$. The function $V$ cannot take $-\infty$ anywhere. If it did, combining that point with a point of its effective domain on the opposite side of zero would force $V(0)=-\infty$. It is therefore proper, and existence of supporting slopes gives $p_1,\ldots,p_{r-1}$ with $V(z)\geq V(0)+\sum_{i<r}\langle p_i,z_iangle$. Set $p_r=p-\sum_{i<r}p_i$. Substituting arbitrary $x_i=x+z_i$ in this inequality yields
\[\sum_i igl(F_i(x_i)-\langle p_i,x_iangle igr)\geq V(0).\]
Taking independent infima proves $\sum_iF_i^*(p_i)\leq-V(0)=(\sum_iF_i)^*(p)$. Together with the first inequality this is equality. If the conjugate on the left is $+\infty$, the first inequality forces every decomposition cost to be $+\infty$, so the formula still holds. See [ Theorem 16.4 , Roc70 ] for the proof. Proposition 21.11.38 . 6FCC352452C3 Let $P\subseteq M$ be a convex body 1 and $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. The following are equivalent: 2A7BEBC1BA5F $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$; 4DF22CEDD6E4 $\operatorname{Dom}F=N$ and $F^*|_{M\setminus P}\equiv \infty $; 97FA12796841 $\operatorname{Dom}F=N$ and $

Moreover, under these conditions, D5ABA398BA7B 21.11.39  egin{equation}  F(n)-\operatorname{Supp}_ P(n)\leq F(0),\quad  orall n\in N. \end{equation} 1. ↩ Here a convex body refers to a non-empty compact convex subset, not necessarily having non-empty interior. Proof. 1 $\implies $ 2 . It is clear that $\operatorname{Dom}F=N$ since $\operatorname{Dom}\operatorname{Supp}_ P=N$. From $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$ and example 21.11.25 , we know that \[  \chi _ P=\operatorname{Supp}_ P^*\preceq F^*.  \] So 2 follows. 2 $\implies $ 3 . This follows from proposition 21.11.34 . 3 $\implies $ 1 . The function $t\mapsto F(tn)$ is convex on $[0,1]$, hence absolutely continuous and differentiable almost everywhere. For almost every $t\in (0,1)$, \[   rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}F(tn)=\partial _ n F(tn) \leq \operatorname{Supp}_ P(n)  \] by theorem 21.11.33 and the assumption $
abla F(N)\subseteq P$. Integrating in $t$ gives \[  F(n)-F(0)\leq \operatorname{Supp}_ P(n).  \] In particular, ( 21.11.39 ) also follows. $\square$

title: Corollary 21.11.26
text: Corollary 21.11.26 . 8C4DFDD0ADE0 Let $F\colon (0,\infty )\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a convex function. If we define $G\colon \mathbb {R}\rightarrow (-\infty ,\infty ]$ by \[  G(\tau )=\sup _{t>0} \Bigl ( t\tau -F(t) \Bigr ),  \] then $G$ is a convex function and E918B6149A40 21.11.27 \begin{equation}  F(t)=G^*(t),\quad \forall t>0. \end{equation} Moreover, 3B0DC2BF53F0 21.11.28 \begin{equation}  G(\tau )=\sup _{t\in \mathbb {R}_{>0}} \Bigl ( t\tau -F(t) \Bigr )=\sup _{t\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}} \Bigl ( t\tau -F(t) \Bigr ). \end{equation} Proof. We distinguish two cases. First suppose that $F(t)=-\infty $ for some $t>0$. Then $F(t)=-\infty $ for all $t>0$ by the convexity of $F$. Our assertions are clear in this case. Next assume that $F(t)\neq -\infty $ for all $t>0$. In this case, theorem 21.11.17 guarantees that $F$ admits a closed proper extension $\tilde{F}\in \mathrm{Conv}(\mathbb {R})$ with \[  \tilde{F}(t)=\infty ,\quad \forall t<0.  \] It follows from ( 21.11.23 ) that \[  G(\tau )=\tilde{F}^*(\tau ),\quad \forall \tau \in \mathbb {R}.  \] Now theorem 21.11.24 implies ( 21.11.27 ). Finally ( 21.11.28 ) follows from the continuity of $F$. $\square$

title: Proposition 21.11.29
text: Proposition 21.11.29 . C3CC440747D6 Let $F\colon N\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$. Define $F^*\colon M\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ by \[  F^*(m)\coloneqq \sup _{n\in N} \left( \langle m,n \rangle -F(n) \right).  \] Then \[  F^*=(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{CE}F)^*.  \] Proof. Put $H=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{CE}F$. Since $H\leq F$, order reversal gives $H^*\geq F^*$. Fix $p$ with $F^*(p)$ finite. The affine function $\ell(x)=\langle p,x\rangle-F^*(p)$ lies below $F$, hence below its convex envelope and below its lower semicontinuous regularization, because $\ell$ itself is continuous. Thus $\langle p,x\rangle-H(x)\leq F^*(p)$ for all $x$, proving $H^*(p)\leq F^*(p)$. If $F^*(p)=+\infty$, the reverse inequality already gives equality. If $F^*(p)=-\infty$, then $F$ is identically $+\infty$; its closed convex envelope is also identically $+\infty$, and the equality is immediate. This treats every possible value of the conjugate.

title: Definition 21.11.30
text:
Definition 21.11.30 . D6A0CB1B8846 Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ and $n\in N$. An element $m\in M$ is a subgradient (in the sense of Alexandrov) of $F$ at $n$ if F6F028287E9D 21.11.31  egin{equation}  F(n')\geq F(n)+\langle n'-n,m angle ,\quad  orall n'\in N. \end{equation} The set of subgradients of $F$ at $n$ is denoted by $
abla F(n)$. More generally, for any subset $E\subseteq N$, we write \[  
abla F(E)= igcup _{n\in E}
abla F(n).  \]

title: Equation 21.11.31
text: F6F028287E9D 21.11.31 \begin{equation}  F(n')\geq F(n)+\langle n'-n,m \rangle ,\quad \forall n'\in N. \end{equation}

title: Definition 21.11.32
text: Definition 21.11.32 . 08E83421373C Given $F,F'\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$, we write $F\preceq _ P F'$ if \[  \overline{\nabla F(N)}\subseteq \overline{\nabla F'(N)}.  \] We write $F\sim _ P F'$ if $F\preceq _ P F'$ and $F'\preceq _ P F$.

title: Theorem 21.11.33
text:
Theorem 21.11.33 . A57F525B7ABC Suppose that $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then the following hold: 8BEAD5D03F60 For any $n
ot\in \operatorname{Dom}F$, $
abla F(n)=\varnothing $; C38BB55E74AA for any $n\in \operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F$, $
abla F(n)
eq \varnothing $; moreover, for any $n'\in N$, we have \[  \partial _{n'} F(n)=\sup \left\{ \langle n', m angle : m\in 
abla F(n)ight\} ;  \] 891D0FE828BD for $n\in N$, the set $
abla F(n)$ is non-empty and bounded if and only if $n\in \operatorname{Int}\operatorname{Dom}F$. Proof. Subgradients at points outside the effective domain are empty by definition. On the relative interior, existence and the directional formula follow from local convex regularity applied in the affine span $A$ of the domain. To view a subgradient as a functional on $N$, extend its restriction to the direction space of $A$ by a linear functional. Any functional vanishing on that direction space may be added without changing the subgradient inequality. Thus for a direction outside that space the supremum in the directional formula is $+\infty$, just as the one-sided directional derivative is; for tangent directions it is the relative formula. At an interior point of the domain, local Lipschitz continuity bounds all subgradients: if $|F(x+v)-F(x)|\leq L|v|$ for small $v$, the subgradient inequality for $v$ and $-v$ gives $|\langle p,vangle|\leq L|v|$, hence $|p|\leq L$. Conversely, suppose the subgradient set is nonempty at a point $x$ of the domain which is not interior. A supporting hyperplane to the closure of the convex domain at $x$ supplies a nonzero $q$ with $\langle q,y-xangle\leq0$ for every $y$ in the domain. If $p$ is a subgradient, then so is $p+tq$ for every $t\geq0$, so the set is unbounded. Supporting hyperplanes also exist when the domain lies in a proper affine subspace, by taking an annihilating functional. This proves the final equivalence.

title: Proposition 21.11.34
text:
Proposition 21.11.34 . 8B18F2B2DE3B Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then \[  
abla F(N)\subseteq \operatorname{Dom}F^*.  \] If moreover $F$ is closed, we have C0D69D19C109 21.11.35  egin{equation}  \operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F^*\subseteq 
abla F(N). \end{equation} In particular, if $F$ is a proper closed convex function on $N$, then \[  \overline{
abla F(N)}=\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F^*}.  \] Proof. If $p\in\partial F(x)$, the subgradient inequality gives $F^*(p)=\langle p,xangle-F(x)<+\infty$, proving the first inclusion. Now assume $F$ is closed and let $p$ lie in the relative interior of $\operatorname{Dom}F^*$. The conjugate is closed and proper by Fenchel duality , so it has a subgradient $x$ at $p$. The same duality theorem gives $p\in\partial F(x)$. Thus the relative interior is contained in the subgradient image. Taking closures in the two inclusions and using that a nonempty convex set has the same closure as its relative interior proves the equality of closures.

title: Equation 21.11.35
text: C0D69D19C109 21.11.35 \begin{equation}  \operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F^*\subseteq \nabla F(N). \end{equation}

title: Proposition 21.11.36
text: Proposition 21.11.36 . 7A76E56311F5 Let $\{ F_ i\} _{i\in I}$ be a non-empty family in $\mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then \[  \left(\bigwedge _{i\in I} F_ i\right)^*=\bigvee _{i\in I} F_ i^*,\quad \left(\bigvee _{i\in I} \operatorname{cl}F_ i\right)^*=\operatorname{cl}\bigwedge _{i\in I} F_ i^*.  \] If $I$ is finite and $\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F_ i}$ is independent of the choice of $i\in I$, then \[  \left(\bigvee _{i\in I} F_ i\right)^*=\bigwedge _{i\in I} F_ i^*.  \]

title: Proposition 21.11.37
text:
Proposition 21.11.37 . 36CA6A68994E Let $F_1,\ldots ,F_ r\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$ ($r\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$). Assume that \[  \bigcap _{i=1}^ r\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}(F_ i)\neq \varnothing ,  \] then for any $m\in M$, \[  \left( \sum _{i=1}^ r F_ i \right)^*(m)=\inf \left\{ \sum _{i=1}^ r F_ i^*(m_ i):m_1,\ldots ,m_ r\in M, \sum _{i=1}^ r m_ i=m \right\} .  \] Proof. For every decomposition $p=\sum_i p_i$, the defining inequalities for the conjugates give $(\sum_iF_i)^*(p)\leq\sum_iF_i^*(p_i)$. It remains to prove the reverse inequality when the left side is finite. The case $r=1$ is immediate. For $r\geq2$, put
\[V(z_1,\ldots,z_{r-1})=\inf_x\left\{\sum_{i<r}F_i(x+z_i)+F_r(x)-\langle p,x\rangle\right\}.\]
This is convex, being an infimum over the fibers of a convex epigraph. Its value at zero is $-(\sum_iF_i)^*(p)$, which is finite. Choose $x_0$ in the common relative interior in the hypothesis. The product of the effective domains has $(x_0,\ldots,x_0)$ in its relative interior. The linear map $(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\mapsto(x_1-x_r,\ldots,x_{r-1}-x_r)$ maps a relative neighborhood of this point onto a relative neighborhood of zero in its image affine span: a surjective linear map between finite-dimensional spaces has a continuous linear right inverse. Consequently zero lies in the relative interior of $\operatorname{Dom}V$. The function $V$ cannot take $-\infty$ anywhere. If it did, combining that point with a point of its effective domain on the opposite side of zero would force $V(0)=-\infty$. It is therefore proper, and existence of supporting slopes gives $p_1,\ldots,p_{r-1}$ with $V(z)\geq V(0)+\sum_{i<r}\langle p_i,z_i\rangle$. Set $p_r=p-\sum_{i<r}p_i$. Substituting arbitrary $x_i=x+z_i$ in this inequality yields
\[\sum_i\bigl(F_i(x_i)-\langle p_i,x_i\rangle\bigr)\geq V(0).\]
Taking independent infima proves $\sum_iF_i^*(p_i)\leq-V(0)=(\sum_iF_i)^*(p)$. Together with the first inequality this is equality. If the conjugate on the left is $+\infty$, the first inequality forces every decomposition cost to be $+\infty$, so the formula still holds.

title: Proposition 21.11.38
text: Proposition 21.11.38 . 6FCC352452C3 Let $P\subseteq M$ be a convex body 1 and $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. The following are equivalent: 2A7BEBC1BA5F $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$; 4DF22CEDD6E4 $\operatorname{Dom}F=N$ and $F^*|_{M\setminus P}\equiv \infty $; 97FA12796841 $\operatorname{Dom}F=N$ and $\nabla F(N)\subseteq P$. Moreover, under these conditions, D5ABA398BA7B 21.11.39 \begin{equation}  F(n)-\operatorname{Supp}_ P(n)\leq F(0),\quad \forall n\in N. \end{equation} 1. ↩ Here a convex body refers to a non-empty compact convex subset, not necessarily having non-empty interior. Proof. 1 $\implies $ 2 . It is clear that $\operatorname{Dom}F=N$ since $\operatorname{Dom}\operatorname{Supp}_ P=N$. From $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$ and example 21.11.25 , we know that \[  \chi _ P=\operatorname{Supp}_ P^*\preceq F^*.  \] So 2 follows. 2 $\implies $ 3 . This follows from proposition 21.11.34 . 3 $\implies $ 1 . The function $t\mapsto F(tn)$ is convex on $[0,1]$, hence absolutely continuous and differentiable almost everywhere. For almost every $t\in (0,1)$, \[  \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}F(tn)=\partial _ n F(tn) \leq \operatorname{Supp}_ P(n)  \] by theorem 21.11.33 and the assumption $\nabla F(N)\subseteq P$. Integrating in $t$ gives \[  F(n)-F(0)\leq \operatorname{Supp}_ P(n).  \] In particular, ( 21.11.39 ) also follows. $\square$

title: Equation 21.11.39
text: D5ABA398BA7B 21.11.39 \begin{equation}  F(n)-\operatorname{Supp}_ P(n)\leq F(0),\quad \forall n\in N. \end{equation}

title: 21.11.40 Classes of convex functions
Definition 21.11.41
text: Definition 21.11.41 . 2AEBD4E3830A We define the set $\mathcal{P}(N,P)$ as the set of proper convex functions $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ such that $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$. We define the set $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(N,P)$ as the set of closed convex functions $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ such that $F\sim \operatorname{Supp}_ P$. We define the set $\mathcal{E}(N,P)$ as follows: Suppose that $\operatorname{Int}P=\varnothing $. Then $\mathcal{E}(N,P)\coloneqq \mathcal{P}(N,P)$; otherwise, let \[  \mathcal{E}(N,P)=\left\{ F\in \mathcal{P}(N,P) : P=\overline{\nabla F(N)} \right\} .  \] We define the set $\mathcal{E}^1(N,P)$ as the subset of $\mathcal{E}(N,P)$ consisting of $F\in \mathcal{E}(N,P)$ with \[  \int _ P F^*\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}<\infty ,  \] where $\mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}$ is any Lebesgue measure on $M$.

title: Proposition 21.11.42
text:
Proposition 21.11.42 . A63267E9EA69 We have \[  \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(N,P)\subseteq \mathcal{E}^{1}(N,P)\subseteq \mathcal{E}(N,P) \subseteq \mathcal{P}(N,P).  \] Proof. When $\operatorname{Int}P=\varnothing $, the assertion is clear. We assume that $\operatorname{Int}P
eq \varnothing $. The second inclusion follows from the definition. We only handle the first inequality. Take $F\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(N,P)$. By definition, $F\sim \operatorname{Supp}_ P$ and hence $F^*\sim \chi _ P$. It follows that $P=\operatorname{Dom}F^*$. By proposition 21.11.38 , we already know that \[  
abla F(N)\subseteq P=\operatorname{Dom}F^*.  \] On the other hand, by proposition 21.11.34 , we have \[  \operatorname{Int}P\subseteq 
abla F(N).  \] So it follows that \[  P=\overline{
abla F(N)}.  \] It is clear that $F^*\sim \chi _ P$ is integrable. $\square$

title: Proposition 21.11.43
text: Proposition 21.11.43 . 281F97D00D5D For any $F\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(N,P)$, we have $F^*|_{M\setminus P}\equiv \infty $ and $F^*$ is bounded on $P$. Proof. From $F\sim \operatorname{Supp}_ P$, we take the Legendre transform to get $F^*\sim \operatorname{Supp}_ P^*=\chi _ P$, where we applied example 21.11.25 . $\square$

title: Definition 21.11.44
text: Definition 21.11.44 . 0E804C9E9F89 We endow the topology of pointwise convergence on $\mathcal{P}(N,P)$.

title: Proposition 21.11.45
text: Proposition 21.11.45 . C0908AA2E3B2 Let $F\in \mathcal{P}(N,P)$. Then there is a decreasing sequence $F_ j\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(N,P)\cap C^{\infty }(N)$ converging to $F$. Proof. Apply the proved decreasing smooth approximation with fixed growth body . It gives smooth convex $F_j$ with bounded difference from the support function of $P$, decreasing pointwise, in fact locally uniformly, to $F$. The bounded-difference condition is precisely membership in $\mathcal E^\infty(N,P)$, and $\mathcal P(N,P)$ is the same upper-growth class in both formulations. That construction preserves the common growth body $P$, including when $P$ has empty interior; therefore the empty-interior case requires no full-dimensional approximation of $P$.

title: Proposition 21.11.46
text: Proposition 21.11.46 . 93CDDD09D6B0 For any $F\in \mathcal{P}(N,P)$, we have \[  \max _{N}(F-\operatorname{Supp}_ P)=F(0).  \] Proof. It follows from ( 21.11.39 ) that \[  \sup _{N}(F-\operatorname{Supp}_ P)\leq F(0).  \] The equality is clearly obtained at $0\in N$. $\square$

title: Lemma 21.11.47
Equation 21.11.48
text: B39039E9725D 21.11.48 \begin{equation}  \overline{\operatorname{Dom}(F+F')^*}=\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F^*}+\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F'{}^*}. \end{equation}

title: 21.11.49 Monge–Ampère measures
Definition 21.11.50
text: Definition 21.11.50 . FF5885207F9E Let $F$ be a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb {R}}$. We define the real Monge–Ampère measure $\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}F$ as the Alexandrov measure on $N_{\mathbb {R}}$ given as follows: for each Borel measurable set $E\subseteq N_{\mathbb {R}}$, define 54CA724C5825 21.11.51 \begin{equation}  \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}F(E)\coloneqq n!\int _{\nabla F(E)} \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}. \end{equation} The measurability and countable additivity in this definition are standard properties of the subgradient map; see for example [ Section 2.1 , Fig17 ] .

title: Equation 21.11.51
text: 54CA724C5825 21.11.51 \begin{equation}  \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}F(E)\coloneqq n!\int _{\nabla F(E)} \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}. \end{equation}

title: Proposition 21.11.52
text: Proposition 21.11.52 . 84CD4F8DE81D Suppose that $F\in C^{1,1}(N_{\mathbb {R}})\cap \mathrm{Conv}(N_{\mathbb {R}})$. Fix an identification $N=\mathbb {Z}^ n$. Then \[  \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}F=n!\cdot \det \nabla ^2 F \, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}.  \] Proof. The measure normalization here is $n!$ times the Lebesgue measure of the subgradient image. The density formula for locally $C^{1,1}$ convex functions proves that this measure is $n!\det D^2F\,\mathrm dx$. Its hypotheses hold because $C^{1,1}$ implies that the gradient is locally Lipschitz, and the lattice coordinates identify $\mathrm dx$ with the normalized $\mathrm d\operatorname{vol}$. The Hessian is its almost-everywhere derivative, equivalently the density of the distributional Hessian. Thus the formula includes nonsmooth $C^{1,1}$ functions and has the required factor $n!$.

title: Proposition 21.11.53
Equation 21.11.54
text: 492151B44AFA 21.11.54 \begin{equation}  \int _{N_{\mathbb {R}}}\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}F=n! \operatorname{vol}P. \end{equation}

title: Theorem 21.11.55
text: Theorem 21.11.55 . 2DC9BC6F295A Let $F,F_ j\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P)$ ($j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$). Assume that $F_ j\to F$. Then \[  \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}(F_ j)\rightharpoonup \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}(F)  \] weakly. Qualification and proof. The topology on $\mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ is pointwise convergence. Since all these functions are finite and convex, local uniform convergence of convex functions shows that $F_j\to F$ uniformly on compact subsets. Alexandrov-measure continuity now gives convergence against every compactly supported continuous test function, that is, weak convergence as Radon measures on this noncompact space. Convergence against all bounded continuous functions would require an additional no-loss-of-mass condition and is not automatic here. For example, on $\mathbb R$ the functions $F_j(x)=\log(1+\exp(x-j))$ have common growth body $[0,1]$ and converge locally uniformly to $0$, while their real Monge--Ampère measures have total mass $1$ and move to $+\infty$. Their vague limit is zero. Thus the weak topology in this assertion must be read as the compactly supported test-function topology; if total masses also converge, a compact-cutoff argument upgrades it to the bounded-continuous topology.

title: Theorem 21.11.56
Lemma 21.11.57
text:
Lemma 21.11.57 . 8DE662F4EFE6 Let $F\in \mathcal{E}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P)$ and set $G=F^*$. Then the map $
abla G$ pushes forward $n!\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}|_{P}$ to $\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$. Equivalently, for every bounded Borel function $h$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$, \[  \int _{N_{\mathbb R}} h\, \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)= n!\int _ P h(
abla G(m))\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}(m).  \] Proof. If $\operatorname{vol}P=0$, the assertion is clear from proposition 21.11.38 and the definition of $\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}$. We may therefore assume that $P$ has non-empty interior. Since $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$, we have $\operatorname{Dom}G\subseteq P$ by proposition 21.11.38 . On the other hand, by the definition of $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ and proposition 21.11.34 , \[  P=\overline{
abla F(N_{\mathbb R})}\subseteq \overline{\operatorname{Dom}G}.  \] Hence $\overline{\operatorname{Dom}G}=P$. Since $\operatorname{Dom}G$ is convex, $G$ is finite on $\operatorname{Int}P$ and is equal to $\infty $ outside $P$. Let $D$ be the set of points in $\operatorname{Int}P$ at which $G$ is differentiable. By [ Theorem 25.5 , Roc70 ] , $P\setminus D$ has measure zero. By [ Theorem 23.5 , Roc70 ] , $m\in 
abla F(n)$ if and only if $n\in 
abla G(m)$. Hence for any Borel set $E\subseteq N_{\mathbb R}$, \[  \{ m\in D:
abla G(m)\in E\} =D\cap 
abla F(E).  \] It follows from definition 21.11.50 that \[  n!\operatorname{vol}\{ m\in P:
abla G(m)\in E\} =n!\operatorname{vol}
abla F(E)=\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)(E).  \] Our assertions follow. $\square$

title: Theorem 21.11.58
text: Theorem 21.11.58 . 59E2455286B4 There is a symmetric map assigning to every $n$-tuple of finite convex functions $F_1,\ldots ,F_ n$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$ a positive Radon measure \[  \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)  \] on $N_{\mathbb R}$ with the following properties: CFA77F02E2A6 For every $q\in \mathbb Z_{>0}$, finite convex functions $F_1,\ldots ,F_ q$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$, and $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ q\geq 0$, \[  \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(\lambda _1F_1+\cdots +\lambda _ qF_ q) =\sum _{i_1,\ldots ,i_ n=1}^ q \lambda _{i_1}\cdots \lambda _{i_ n} \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_{i_1},\ldots ,F_{i_ n}).  \] 72A14F74D8A4 For every finite convex function $F$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$, \[  \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F,\ldots ,F)=\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F).  \] 0430553123BF The map $\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}$ is additive and positively homogeneous of degree $1$ in each entry. In other words, for finite convex functions $F,G,F_2,\ldots ,F_ n$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$ and $\lambda ,\mu \geq 0$, \[  \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(\lambda F+\mu G,F_2,\ldots ,F_ n) =\lambda \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F,F_2,\ldots ,F_ n) +\mu \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(G,F_2,\ldots ,F_ n).  \] Proof. The construction of mixed Alexandrov measures gives a positive, symmetric, additive and positively homogeneous measure in the $n$ arguments, with diagonal equal to the Alexandrov measure defined here. Repeatedly expand the diagonal measure of $\sum_i\lambda_iF_i$ using this additivity and homogeneity. Each ordered choice $(i_1,\ldots,i_n)$ contributes $\lambda_{i_1}\cdots\lambda_{i_n}\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_{i_1},\ldots,F_{i_n})$, which is the asserted polynomial formula. The earlier proof first verifies positivity for smooth convex functions using mixed determinants, and then uses convolution and local uniform continuity of the diagonal measure to pass to finite convex functions. In particular positivity is proved rather than inferred from a signed polarization formula. Uniqueness follows by recovering each coefficient from the diagonal polynomial, for instance by polarization. The normalization remains $n!$ on the diagonal.

title: 21.11.59 Several lemmata
text: Lemma 21.11.60 . B1B557E6282F Let $\alpha ,\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m\in \mathbb {Z}^ n$. Let $\Delta $ be the polytope generated by $\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m$. Then the following are equivalent: 45E8CA3F6710 EF4C4E285442 21.11.61 \begin{equation}  |z^{\alpha }|^2\left(\sum _{i=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ i}|^2 \right)^{-1} \end{equation} is a bounded function on $\mathbb {C}^{*n}$. B62429A6EB39 $\alpha \in \Delta $. Proof. 2 $\implies $ 1 . Write $\alpha =\sum _ i t_ i\beta _ i$, where $t_ i\in [0,1]$, $\sum _ i t_ i=1$. Then \[  \begin{aligned}  |z^{\alpha }|^2\left(\sum _{i=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ i}|^2 \right)^{-1} & =\prod _ i |z^{\beta _ i}|^{2t_ i}\left(\sum _{i=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ i}|^2 \right)^{-1}\\ & \leq \prod _ i\left(\sum _{j=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ j}|^2\right)^{t_ i} \left(\sum _{i=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ i}|^2 \right)^{-1}=1. \end{aligned}  \] 1 $\implies $ 2 . Assume that $\alpha \not\in \Delta $. By the strict separation theorem, there is $a=(a_1,\ldots ,a_ n)\in \mathbb {R}^ n$ such that \[  a\cdot \alpha >\max _ i a\cdot \beta _ i.  \] Set \[  z(t)\coloneqq (t^{a_1},\ldots ,t^{a_ n}).  \] Then ( 21.11.61 ) evaluated at $z(t)$ grows like \[  \frac{t^{2a\cdot \alpha }}{\sum _ i t^{2a\cdot \beta _ i}}  \] as $t\to \infty $, and hence is not bounded. $\square$ Lemma 21.11.62 . 81D915E5313D Let $\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m\in \mathbb {N}^ n$ and $\beta \in \mathbb {R}^ n$. Then the following are equivalent: EE49D9E1DF50 $\log \sum _{i=1}^ m \mathrm{e}^{x\cdot \beta _ i}-x\cdot \beta $ is bounded from below. BD8E8347B6CF $\beta $ is in the convex hull of the $\beta _ i$'s. Proof. If $\beta =\sum _ i t_ i\beta _ i$ with $t_ i\in [0,1]$ and $\sum _ i t_ i=1$, then by the weighted arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, \[  x\cdot \beta =\sum _ i t_ i\, x\cdot \beta _ i \leq \log \sum _ i t_ i\mathrm{e}^{x\cdot \beta _ i} \leq \log \sum _ i \mathrm{e}^{x\cdot \beta _ i}.  \] This proves that the function in 1 is bounded from below. Conversely, if $\beta $ does not lie in the convex hull of the $\beta _ i$'s, choose $a\in \mathbb {R}^ n$ such that \[  a\cdot \beta >\max _ i a\cdot \beta _ i.  \] Evaluating at $x=ta$ and letting $t\to \infty $, we find \[  \log \sum _ i \mathrm{e}^{t a\cdot \beta _ i}-t\, a\cdot \beta \to -\infty ,  \] contradicting 1 . $\square$ Lemma 21.11.63 . 66B643EAC79A Let $I\subseteq \mathbb {R}$ be an open interval containing $0$. Let $(f_ k\colon I\rightarrow \mathbb {R})_{k\geq 1}$ be a sequence of convex functions, and let $g\colon I\to \mathbb {R}$ be a function. Assume that \[  \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } f_ k(t)\leq g(t)\quad \text{for every } t\in I,  \] and that \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } f_ k(0)=g(0).  \] If each $f_ k$ and $g$ is differentiable at $0$, then \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0)=g'(0).  \] Proof. Since $f_ k$ is convex and differentiable at $0$, for every $t\in I$, \[  f_ k(t)\geq f_ k(0)+t f_ k'(0).  \] Taking the upper limit as $k\to \infty $ and using the assumptions gives \[  \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } t f_ k'(0) \leq g(t)-g(0).  \] For $t>0$, this yields \[  \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0) \leq \frac{g(t)-g(0)}{t}.  \] Letting $t\to 0+$ and using the differentiability of $g$ at $0$, we get \[  \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0)\leq g'(0).  \] For $t<0$, the same inequality gives \[  \varliminf _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0) \geq \frac{g(t)-g(0)}{t}.  \] Letting $t\to 0-$ and again using the differentiability of $g$ at $0$, we obtain \[  \varliminf _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0)\geq g'(0).  \] Therefore \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0)=g'(0),  \] as claimed. $\square$

title: Lemma 21.11.60
text: Lemma 21.11.60 . B1B557E6282F Let $\alpha ,\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m\in \mathbb {Z}^ n$. Let $\Delta $ be the polytope generated by $\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m$. Then the following are equivalent: 45E8CA3F6710 EF4C4E285442 21.11.61 \begin{equation}  |z^{\alpha }|^2\left(\sum _{i=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ i}|^2 \right)^{-1} \end{equation} is a bounded function on $\mathbb {C}^{*n}$. B62429A6EB39 $\alpha \in \Delta $. Proof. 2 $\implies $ 1 . Write $\alpha =\sum _ i t_ i\beta _ i$, where $t_ i\in [0,1]$, $\sum _ i t_ i=1$. Then \[  \begin{aligned}  |z^{\alpha }|^2\left(\sum _{i=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ i}|^2 \right)^{-1} & =\prod _ i |z^{\beta _ i}|^{2t_ i}\left(\sum _{i=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ i}|^2 \right)^{-1}\\ & \leq \prod _ i\left(\sum _{j=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ j}|^2\right)^{t_ i} \left(\sum _{i=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ i}|^2 \right)^{-1}=1. \end{aligned}  \] 1 $\implies $ 2 . Assume that $\alpha \not\in \Delta $. By the strict separation theorem, there is $a=(a_1,\ldots ,a_ n)\in \mathbb {R}^ n$ such that \[  a\cdot \alpha >\max _ i a\cdot \beta _ i.  \] Set \[  z(t)\coloneqq (t^{a_1},\ldots ,t^{a_ n}).  \] Then ( 21.11.61 ) evaluated at $z(t)$ grows like \[  \frac{t^{2a\cdot \alpha }}{\sum _ i t^{2a\cdot \beta _ i}}  \] as $t\to \infty $, and hence is not bounded. $\square$

title: Lemma 21.11.62
text: Lemma 21.11.62 . 81D915E5313D Let $\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m\in \mathbb {N}^ n$ and $\beta \in \mathbb {R}^ n$. Then the following are equivalent: EE49D9E1DF50 $\log \sum _{i=1}^ m \mathrm{e}^{x\cdot \beta _ i}-x\cdot \beta $ is bounded from below. BD8E8347B6CF $\beta $ is in the convex hull of the $\beta _ i$'s. Proof. If $\beta =\sum _ i t_ i\beta _ i$ with $t_ i\in [0,1]$ and $\sum _ i t_ i=1$, then by the weighted arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, \[  x\cdot \beta =\sum _ i t_ i\, x\cdot \beta _ i \leq \log \sum _ i t_ i\mathrm{e}^{x\cdot \beta _ i} \leq \log \sum _ i \mathrm{e}^{x\cdot \beta _ i}.  \] This proves that the function in 1 is bounded from below. Conversely, if $\beta $ does not lie in the convex hull of the $\beta _ i$'s, choose $a\in \mathbb {R}^ n$ such that \[  a\cdot \beta >\max _ i a\cdot \beta _ i.  \] Evaluating at $x=ta$ and letting $t\to \infty $, we find \[  \log \sum _ i \mathrm{e}^{t a\cdot \beta _ i}-t\, a\cdot \beta \to -\infty ,  \] contradicting 1 . $\square$

title: Lemma 21.11.63
text: Lemma 21.11.63 . 66B643EAC79A Let $I\subseteq \mathbb {R}$ be an open interval containing $0$. Let $(f_ k\colon I\rightarrow \mathbb {R})_{k\geq 1}$ be a sequence of convex functions, and let $g\colon I\to \mathbb {R}$ be a function. Assume that \[  \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } f_ k(t)\leq g(t)\quad \text{for every } t\in I,  \] and that \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } f_ k(0)=g(0).  \] If each $f_ k$ and $g$ is differentiable at $0$, then \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0)=g'(0).  \] Proof. Since $f_ k$ is convex and differentiable at $0$, for every $t\in I$, \[  f_ k(t)\geq f_ k(0)+t f_ k'(0).  \] Taking the upper limit as $k\to \infty $ and using the assumptions gives \[  \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } t f_ k'(0) \leq g(t)-g(0).  \] For $t>0$, this yields \[  \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0) \leq \frac{g(t)-g(0)}{t}.  \] Letting $t\to 0+$ and using the differentiability of $g$ at $0$, we get \[  \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0)\leq g'(0).  \] For $t<0$, the same inequality gives \[  \varliminf _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0) \geq \frac{g(t)-g(0)}{t}.  \] Letting $t\to 0-$ and again using the differentiability of $g$ at $0$, we obtain \[  \varliminf _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0)\geq g'(0).  \] Therefore \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0)=g'(0),  \] as claimed. $\square$

title: 9.10 Pluripotential theory on unibranch spaces
text: This appendix explains how much of the pluripotential theory developed in the body of the book extends from compact Kähler manifolds to compact unibranch Kähler spaces. The unibranch hypothesis is the natural generality in which plurisubharmonic functions descend through resolutions and the basic envelope formalism remains meaningful. Some constructions, especially the trace operator of section 20.2 , require extra care in the singular setting; we record here the precise statements needed in the main text.

title: 9.10.1 Complex spaces
text:
A complex space is assumed to be reduced, Hausdorff and paracompact here. Definition 9.10.2 . F30317C89D08 A prime divisor over an irreducible complex space $Z$ is a connected smooth hypersurface $E\subseteq X'$, where $X'\rightarrow Z$ is a proper bimeromorphic morphism with $X'$ smooth. Such a morphism $X'\rightarrow Z$ is also called a resolution of $Z$. The center of the prime divisor is defined as the image of $E$ in $Z$. Two prime divisors $E_1\subseteq X'_1$ and $E_2\subseteq X'_2$ over $Z$ are equivalent if there is a common resolution $X''\rightarrow Z$ dominating both $X_1'$ and $X_2'$ such that the strict transforms of $E_1$ and $E_2$ coincide. The set $Z^{\operatorname{div}}$ is the set of pairs $(c,E)$, where $c\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$ and $E$ is an equivalence class of a prime divisor over $Z$. For simplicity, we will denote the pair $(c,E)$ by $c\operatorname{ord}_ E$, although one should not really think of this object as a valuation unless $Z$ is projective and irreducible. Note that a prime divisor on $Z$ does not always define a prime divisor over $Z$ if $Z$ is singular. Definition 9.10.3 . 4BA9DE7FEF24 A complex space $X$ is unibranch if for all $x\in X$, the local ring $\mathcal{O}_{X,x}$ is unibranch. See [ Tag 0BPZ , stacks-project ] for the notion of unibranch local rings. In [ CAS ] , the same notion is known as local irreducibility . We prefer the name unibranchness , because the corresponding terminology in algebraic geometry is standard and goes back to Grothendieck [ (0.23.2.1) , EGAIV1 ] . 


The notion of unibranchness coincides with the usual one when $\mathcal{X}$ is an algebraic variety: Proposition 9.10.4 . 1A7FEC3124D0 Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a reduced scheme of finite type over $\mathbb {C}$, and let $\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}}$ be the associated complex space. Then $\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}}$ is unibranch in the sense above if and only if $\mathcal{X}$ is unibranch in the algebraic sense (see [ Tag 0BQ2 , stacks-project ] ). This is [ Remark 2.7 , Xia23Mabuchi ] in the arXiv version. Proof. Let $x\in \mathcal{X}(\mathbb {C})$. Then we claim that $\mathcal{X}$ is unibranch at $x$ if and only if $\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}}$ is unibranch at $x$. By GAGA, there is a natural morphism of ringed spaces $(\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}},\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}}})\rightarrow (\mathcal{X},\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}})$. Then since $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X},x}$ is excellent, $\mathcal{X}$ is unibranch at $x$ if and only if $\widehat{\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X},x}}=\widehat{\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}},x}}$ is integral ( [ Théorème 18.9.1 , EGAIV4 ] ). The latter implies that $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}},x}$ is unibranch by [ Chapitre 5, Exercise 2.8 , AC ] . Running the same argument the other way round, we conclude that $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X},x}$ is unibranch if and only if $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}},x}$ is. $\square$ Theorem 9.10.5 (Zariski's main theorem) . E707851D5DBA Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism between complex spaces. Assume that $X$ is unibranch. Then $\pi $ has connected fibers. We follow [ Proof of Théorème 1.7 , Dem85 ] . Proof. Let $Z\subseteq X$ be the smallest nowhere dense analytic subset such that $\pi $ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus Z$. Assume that the fiber $F=\pi ^{-1}(x)$ over some $x\in X$ is disconnected. Since $\pi $ is proper, $F$ is compact. Choose a decomposition $F=F_1\sqcup F_2$ into two non-empty disjoint compact open subsets of $F$, and choose disjoint open neighborhoods $W_1,W_2$ of $F_1,F_2$ in $Y$. Since proper maps are closed, after shrinking an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$, we may assume that \[  \pi ^{-1}(U)\subseteq W_1\cup W_2.  \] Thus $\pi ^{-1}(U)$ is disconnected. Since $X$ is unibranch, we may shrink $U$ further so that $U$ is irreducible. Then $U\setminus Z$ is connected (cf. [ Chapter 9, §1.2 , CAS ] ). Since $\pi $ is bimeromorphic, every irreducible component of $Y$ maps onto an irreducible component of $X$. Hence $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$ contains no irreducible component of $Y$ and is nowhere dense. On the other hand, write \[  \pi ^{-1}(U)=V_1\sqcup V_2  \] as a union of two non-empty disjoint open subsets. Each $V_ i$ meets $\pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z)$: otherwise $V_ i$ would be a non-empty open subset of $Y$ contained in the nowhere dense analytic subset $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$, which is impossible. Hence \[  \pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z) = \bigl (V_1\cap \pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z)\bigr ) \sqcup \bigl (V_2\cap \pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z)\bigr )  \] is disconnected. This contradicts the fact that $\pi \colon \pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z)\rightarrow U\setminus Z$ is an isomorphism and $U\setminus Z$ is connected. $\square$ Definition 9.10.6 . C9A9F3CE78E7 A modification of a compact complex space $X$ is a finite composition of blow-ups with smooth centers. We say a modification $\pi '\colon Z\rightarrow X$ dominates another $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ if there is a morphism $g\colon Z\rightarrow Y$ of complex spaces making the following diagram commutative: 8D4BB1A6524D 9.10.7 The modifications of $X$ together with the domination relation form a directed set. Theorem 9.10.8 (Hironaka's Chow lemma) . 3CD8BF9158DD Suppose that $X$ is a compact complex space. Then every proper bimeromorphic morphism to $X$ can be dominated by a modification. This follows from the proof of [ Corollary 2 , Hir75 ] . Theorem 9.10.9 . 8F66FA207B82 Let $X$ be a compact complex space. Then there is a modification $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ such that $Y$ is smooth. See [ BM97 , Wlo09 ] . Corollary 9.10.10 . 178E0605C99D Let $X$ be an irreducible compact complex space and $E$ be a prime divisor over $X$. Then there is a modification $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ such that $Y$ is smooth and $E$ can be realized as a prime divisor on $Y$. Proof. Choose a smooth model $X'\rightarrow X$ on which $E$ is realized. By theorem 9.10.8 , this proper bimeromorphic morphism is dominated by a modification $Y\rightarrow X$. After further resolving the pair if necessary, we may assume that $Y$ is smooth and that the strict transform of $E$ on $Y$ is smooth. This strict transform realizes the same prime divisor over $X$. $\square$

Then $\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}}$ is unibranch in the sense above if and only if $\mathcal{X}$ is unibranch in the algebraic sense (see [ Tag 0BQ2 , stacks-project ] ). Proof. Let $x\in \mathcal{X}(\mathbb {C})$. Then we claim that $\mathcal{X}$ is unibranch at $x$ if and only if $\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}}$ is unibranch at $x$. title: Theorem 9.10.5 (Zariski's main theorem)
text: Theorem 9.10.5 (Zariski's main theorem) . E707851D5DBA Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism between complex spaces. Assume that $X$ is unibranch. Then $\pi $ has connected fibers. Proof. Let $Z\subseteq X$ be the smallest nowhere dense analytic subset such that $\pi $ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus Z$. Assume that the fiber $F=\pi ^{-1}(x)$ over some $x\in X$ is disconnected. Since $\pi $ is proper, $F$ is compact. Choose a decomposition $F=F_1\sqcup F_2$ into two non-empty disjoint compact open subsets of $F$, and choose disjoint open neighborhoods $W_1,W_2$ of $F_1,F_2$ in $Y$. Since proper maps are closed, after shrinking an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$, we may assume that \[  \pi ^{-1}(U)\subseteq W_1\cup W_2.  \] Thus $\pi ^{-1}(U)$ is disconnected. Since $X$ is unibranch, we may shrink $U$ further so that $U$ is irreducible. Then $U\setminus Z$ is connected (cf. [ Chapter 9, §1.2 , CAS ] ). Since $\pi $ is bimeromorphic, every irreducible component of $Y$ maps onto an irreducible component of $X$. Hence $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$ contains no irreducible component of $Y$ and is nowhere dense. On the other hand, write \[  \pi ^{-1}(U)=V_1\sqcup V_2  \] as a union of two non-empty disjoint open subsets. Each $V_ i$ meets $\pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z)$: otherwise $V_ i$ would be a non-empty open subset of $Y$ contained in the nowhere dense analytic subset $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$, which is impossible. Hence \[  \pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z) = \bigl (V_1\cap \pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z)\bigr ) \sqcup \bigl (V_2\cap \pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z)\bigr )  \] is disconnected. This contradicts the fact that $\pi \colon \pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z)\rightarrow U\setminus Z$ is an isomorphism and $U\setminus Z$ is connected. $\square$

title: 9.10.11 Plurisubharmonic functions
text:
Let $X$ be a complex space. Definition 9.10.12 . FCF157D7001A A function $\varphi \colon Xightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ is plurisubharmonic if 96254565568F $\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $ on any irreducible component of $X$, and E2E28DC114D3 for any $x\in X$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ in $X$, a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ N$, a closed immersion $V\hookrightarrow \Omega $ and a plurisubharmonic function $	ilde{\varphi }\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ such that $\varphi |_ V=	ilde{\varphi }|_ V$ under this immersion. The set of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Similarly, if $	heta $ is a smooth closed 2 real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, then a function $\varphi \colon Xightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic if for any $x\in X$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ in $X$, a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ N$, a closed immersion $V\hookrightarrow \Omega $ and a smooth function $g$ on $\Omega $ such that $	heta =(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g)|_ V$ and $g|_ V+\varphi |_ V\in \mathrm{PSH}(V)$. 2. ↩ Here closed means that locally $	heta $ is defined by a closed form under a local embedding. Theorem 9.10.13 (Fornaess–Narasimhan) . 48473380B913 Let $\varphi \colon Xightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a function. Assume that $\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $ on any irreducible component of $X$. Then the following are equivalent: C2704BBBABCF $\varphi $ is psh; 917F8CC8F375 $\varphi $ is usc and for any morphism $f\colon \Delta ightarrow X$ from the open unit disk $\Delta $ in $\mathbb {C}$ to $X$ such that $f^*\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $, the pull-back $f^*\varphi $ is subharmonic. See [ FN80 ] . Theorem 9.10.14 (Grauert–Remmert) . C69D2F0ABA4F Let $X$ be a unibranch 3 complex space, let $Z$ be an analytic subset in $X$, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X\setminus Z)$. Then the function $\varphi $ admits an extension to $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ in the following two cases: C2D00AE1EE6E The set $Z$ has codimension at least $2$ everywhere. EC2A3ADCF9E6 The set $Z$ has codimension at least $1$ everywhere and $\varphi $ is locally bounded from above on an open neighborhood of $Z$. In both cases, the extension is unique and is given by B66F47F11DC8 9.10.15  egin{equation}  \varphi (x)=\varlimsup _{X\setminus Z
i y	o x}\varphi (y),\quad x\in X. \end{equation} 3. ↩ Unibranchness is very important here. Otherwise, consider the case where $X$ is the union of two copies of $\mathbb {C}$ intersecting only at their origins, $Z$ is the common origin. If we set $\varphi \equiv 0$ on one punctured plane and $\varphi \equiv 1$ on the other, then it is clear that $\varphi $ cannot be extended to $X$. This leads to a few misleading statements in the modern literature. The problem is that in the early German literature, komplexer Raum is assumed to be either normal or unibranch! The proof given below combines [ Théorème 1.7 , Dem85 ] and [ GR56 ] . 1 1. ↩ This theorem has a quite entangled history. The corresponding results for subharmonic functions are generally attributed to Brelot. In [ GR56 ] , they cited a paper of Brelot written in 1934, which I cannot find. But in 1949, on the very first issue of Annales de l'Institut Fourier , Brelot published a paper [ Bre49 ] with a very similar title, studying the behavior of a subharmonic function on the punctured neighborhood of a point. The general theorem was due to Grauert and Remmert, see [ GR56 ] . Their original proof was quite complicated, due to the fact that resolution of singularities was not available at that time. Later on, in 1985, Demailly published the influential paper [ Dem85 ] and gave a simpler proof. Oddly enough, Demailly did not cite either Grauert–Remmert or Brelot. He did not even mention that this result was already proved by Grauert–Remmert. The paper [ Dem85 ] is so influential that in France few people know the existence of [ GR56 ] . Proof. We first prove the uniqueness, which is a local problem on $X$. Let $\psi $ denote the function defined by the right-hand side of ( 9.10.15 ). If $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ is an extension of $\varphi $, then upper semicontinuity gives $\eta \geq \psi $. Conversely, take $z\in Z$ and a holomorphic map $f\colon \Delta ightarrow X$ such that $f(0)=z$ and $f(\Delta )
ot\subset Z$. From the subharmonicity of $f^*\eta $ and ( 9.10.15 ), we find that \[  \eta (z)=f^*\eta (0)=\varlimsup _{\Delta ^* 
i w	o 0}f^*\eta (w)\leq \varlimsup _{X\setminus Z
i y	o z}\varphi (y)=\psi (z),  \] where the second equality follows from theorem 5.14.10 . Thus $\eta =\psi $, and uniqueness follows. Having established the uniqueness of the extension, the existence also becomes a local problem. So we can freely shrink $X$ around any point in $Z$ in the proof. 2 Let $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ be a resolution of singularities. By the smooth version of the extension theorem theorem 5.14.10 , we know that $\pi ^*\varphi $ admits a unique extension to a psh function on $Y$, which we denote by $\eta $. Note that all fibers of $\pi $ are connected since $X$ is unibranch, thanks to theorem 9.10.5 . Furthermore, the fibers are compact, since $\pi $ is proper. The restriction of $\eta $ to each fiber is psh or identically $-\infty $, hence is constant by the maximum principle applied to a resolution. It therefore descends to an upper semicontinuous function $\psi $ on $X$, and $\psi |_{X\setminus Z}=\varphi $. We verify that $\psi $ is plurisubharmonic using theorem 9.10.13 . Let $f\colon \Delta ightarrow X$ be a holomorphic map. We assume that $f^*\psi 
ot\equiv -\infty $. It suffices to show that $f^*\psi $ is subharmonic at $0\in \Delta $. After replacing $\Delta $ by a finite ramified cover if necessary, the germ of $f$ lifts to $Y$. Indeed, consider the proper projection \[  \Delta 	imes _ X Y\longrightarrow \Delta .  \] Choose an irreducible analytic curve in $\Delta 	imes _ X Y$ passing through a point over $0$ and dominating $\Delta $; after shrinking $\Delta $ and normalizing this curve, we obtain a finite ramified cover of the disk. After replacing $\Delta $ by a smaller disk, there are an integer $k>0$ and a holomorphic map $f'\colon \Delta 	o Y$ such that \[  f(t^ k)=\pi (f'(t)).  \] Therefore, $\psi (f(t^ k))=\eta (f'(t))$ near $0$. Since subharmonicity descends under the finite map $t\mapsto t^ k$, it follows that $f^*\psi $ is subharmonic near $0$. 1 By the local description of complex spaces [ Section 3.4 , CAS ] , we may assume that there is a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$, a finite $s$-sheet branched covering $\Phi \colon Xightarrow \Omega $ with branched locus contained in a proper analytic subset $V\subseteq \Omega $. We may assume that $X$ is connected, $n\geq 1$. It suffices to show that $\varphi $ is locally bounded from above near $Z$, since then 2 applies. Suppose that this fails. Then we can find $z\in Z$ and $x_ i\in X\setminus Z$ ($i\geq 1$) converging to $z$ such that \[  \lim _{i	o \infty } \varphi (x_ i)=\infty .  \] Using ( 9.10.15 ) around each $x_ i$, we may further assume that $x_ i\in X\setminus (\Phi ^{-1}(\Phi (Z)\cup V))$. Let $L$ be a complex line passing through $\Phi (z)$ intersecting $(\Phi (Z)\cup V)\cap \overline{B}$ only at $\Phi (z)$, where $B\Subset B'\Subset \Omega $ are two small open balls centered at $\Phi (z)$. Since $\Phi $ is finite, $\Phi (Z)$ still has codimension at least $2$ in $\Omega $. Hence, for each $i$, the set of directions of lines through $\Phi (x_ i)$ meeting $B'\cap \Phi (Z)$ is contained in a proper analytic subset of the projective space of directions. We can therefore choose lines $L_ i$ through $\Phi (x_ i)$ converging to $L$ such that $L_ i\cap (B'\cap \Phi (Z))=\varnothing $. Moreover, since $\Phi (x_ i)
otin V$, no such $L_ i$ is contained in $V$, and hence $L_ i\cap (B'\cap V)$ is discrete. Then $\Phi $ restricts to a branched covering over $B'\cap L_ i$ for all $i\geq 1$. Adding a constant to $\varphi $, we may assume that $\varphi |_{\Phi ^{-1}(L\cap \partial B)}<0$. We can then find an open neighborhood $U$ of $\Phi ^{-1}(L\cap \partial B)$ so that $\varphi |_ U<0$. For large $i$, we have $\Phi ^{-1}(L_ i\cap \partial B)\subseteq U$ and $\Phi (x_ i)\in B$. Put \[  C_ i\coloneqq \Phi ^{-1}(L_ i\cap B').  \] Thus $C_ i$ is a one-dimensional complex space contained in $X\setminus Z$. Since $\Phi |_{C_ i}$ is finite over $L_ i\cap B'$, the inverse image $C_ i\cap \Phi ^{-1}(\overline B)$ is compact, and its boundary is contained in $\Phi ^{-1}(L_ i\cap \partial B)$. Passing to the normalization of each irreducible component of $C_ i$, the pull-back of $\varphi $ is subharmonic. The one-dimensional maximum principle therefore gives \[  \varphi (x_ i)\leq \sup _{\Phi ^{-1}(L_ i\cap \partial B)}\varphi <0,  \] which is a contradiction. $\square$ Corollary 9.10.16 . 2DA8FD7B7A99 Let $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism between compact Kähler spaces. Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Assume that $X$ is unibranch. Then the pull-back induces a bijection \[  \pi ^*\colon \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )\xlongrightarrow {\sim }\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta ).  \] Proof. Injectivity follows from the surjectivity of $\pi $. For surjectivity, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. The assertion is local on $X$, so after subtracting a local potential of $	heta $ we may assume that $	heta =0$. By theorem 9.10.5 , the fibers of $\pi $ are connected. The restriction of $u$ to any compact fiber is psh, hence is constant by the maximum principle. Thus $u$ descends to a function $v$ on $X$. Since $\pi $ is proper, $v$ is upper semicontinuous. It remains to check that $v$ is psh. By theorem 9.10.13 , it suffices to test on holomorphic disks. Let $f\colon \Delta ightarrow X$ be a holomorphic disk such that $f^*v
ot\equiv -\infty $. As in the proof of theorem 9.10.14 , after a finite ramified cover $ho \colon \Delta ightarrow \Delta $, the germ of $f\circ ho $ lifts to $Y$. The pull-back $(f^*v)\circ ho $ is therefore subharmonic, so $f^*v$ is subharmonic. Hence $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, and the general $	heta $-psh case follows by adding back the local potentials. $\square$

title: Definition 9.10.12
text: Definition 9.10.12 . FCF157D7001A A function $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ is plurisubharmonic if 96254565568F $\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $ on any irreducible component of $X$, and E2E28DC114D3 for any $x\in X$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ in $X$, a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ N$, a closed immersion $V\hookrightarrow \Omega $ and a plurisubharmonic function $\tilde{\varphi }\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ such that $\varphi |_ V=\tilde{\varphi }|_ V$ under this immersion. The set of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Similarly, if $\theta $ is a smooth closed 2 real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, then a function $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic if for any $x\in X$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ in $X$, a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ N$, a closed immersion $V\hookrightarrow \Omega $ and a smooth function $g$ on $\Omega $ such that $\theta =(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g)|_ V$ and $g|_ V+\varphi |_ V\in \mathrm{PSH}(V)$. 2. ↩ Here closed means that locally $\theta $ is defined by a closed form under a local embedding.

title: Theorem 9.10.13 (Fornaess–Narasimhan)
text: Theorem 9.10.13 (Fornaess–Narasimhan) . 48473380B913 Let $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a function. Assume that $\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $ on any irreducible component of $X$. Then the following are equivalent: C2704BBBABCF $\varphi $ is psh; 917F8CC8F375 $\varphi $ is usc and for any morphism $f\colon \Delta \rightarrow X$ from the open unit disk $\Delta $ in $\mathbb {C}$ to $X$ such that $f^*\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $, the pull-back $f^*\varphi $ is subharmonic.

title: Theorem 9.10.14 (Grauert–Remmert)
text:
Theorem 9.10.14 (Grauert–Remmert) . C69D2F0ABA4F Let $X$ be a unibranch 3 complex space, let $Z$ be an analytic subset in $X$, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X\setminus Z)$. Then the function $\varphi $ admits an extension to $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ in the following two cases: C2D00AE1EE6E The set $Z$ has codimension at least $2$ everywhere. EC2A3ADCF9E6 The set $Z$ has codimension at least $1$ everywhere and $\varphi $ is locally bounded from above on an open neighborhood of $Z$. In both cases, the extension is unique and is given by B66F47F11DC8 9.10.15  egin{equation}  \varphi (x)=\varlimsup _{X\setminus Z
i y	o x}\varphi (y),\quad x\in X. \end{equation} 3. ↩ Unibranchness is very important here. Otherwise, consider the case where $X$ is the union of two copies of $\mathbb {C}$ intersecting only at their origins, $Z$ is the common origin. If we set $\varphi \equiv 0$ on one punctured plane and $\varphi \equiv 1$ on the other, then it is clear that $\varphi $ cannot be extended to $X$. This leads to a few misleading statements in the modern literature. The problem is that in the early German literature, komplexer Raum is assumed to be either normal or unibranch! Proof. We first prove the uniqueness, which is a local problem on $X$. Let $\psi $ denote the function defined by the right-hand side of ( 9.10.15 ). If $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ is an extension of $\varphi $, then upper semicontinuity gives $\eta \geq \psi $. Conversely, take $z\in Z$ and a holomorphic map $f\colon \Delta ightarrow X$ such that $f(0)=z$ and $f(\Delta )
ot\subset Z$. From the subharmonicity of $f^*\eta $ and ( 9.10.15 ), we find that \[  \eta (z)=f^*\eta (0)=\varlimsup _{\Delta ^* 
i w	o 0}f^*\eta (w)\leq \varlimsup _{X\setminus Z
i y	o z}\varphi (y)=\psi (z),  \] where the second equality follows from theorem 5.14.10 . Thus $\eta =\psi $, and uniqueness follows. Having established the uniqueness of the extension, the existence also becomes a local problem. So we can freely shrink $X$ around any point in $Z$ in the proof. 2 Let $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ be a resolution of singularities. By the smooth version of the extension theorem theorem 5.14.10 , we know that $\pi ^*\varphi $ admits a unique extension to a psh function on $Y$, which we denote by $\eta $. Note that all fibers of $\pi $ are connected since $X$ is unibranch, thanks to theorem 9.10.5 . Furthermore, the fibers are compact, since $\pi $ is proper. The restriction of $\eta $ to each fiber is psh or identically $-\infty $, hence is constant by the maximum principle applied to a resolution. It therefore descends to an upper semicontinuous function $\psi $ on $X$, and $\psi |_{X\setminus Z}=\varphi $. We verify that $\psi $ is plurisubharmonic using theorem 9.10.13 . Let $f\colon \Delta ightarrow X$ be a holomorphic map. We assume that $f^*\psi 
ot\equiv -\infty $. It suffices to show that $f^*\psi $ is subharmonic at $0\in \Delta $. After replacing $\Delta $ by a finite ramified cover if necessary, the germ of $f$ lifts to $Y$. Indeed, consider the proper projection \[  \Delta 	imes _ X Y\longrightarrow \Delta .  \] Choose an irreducible analytic curve in $\Delta 	imes _ X Y$ passing through a point over $0$ and dominating $\Delta $; after shrinking $\Delta $ and normalizing this curve, we obtain a finite ramified cover of the disk. After replacing $\Delta $ by a smaller disk, there are an integer $k>0$ and a holomorphic map $f'\colon \Delta 	o Y$ such that \[  f(t^ k)=\pi (f'(t)).  \] Therefore, $\psi (f(t^ k))=\eta (f'(t))$ near $0$. Since subharmonicity descends under the finite map $t\mapsto t^ k$, it follows that $f^*\psi $ is subharmonic near $0$. 1 By the local description of complex spaces [ Section 3.4 , CAS ] , we may assume that there is a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$, a finite $s$-sheet branched covering $\Phi \colon Xightarrow \Omega $ with branched locus contained in a proper analytic subset $V\subseteq \Omega $. We may assume that $X$ is connected, $n\geq 1$. It suffices to show that $\varphi $ is locally bounded from above near $Z$, since then 2 applies. Suppose that this fails. Then we can find $z\in Z$ and $x_ i\in X\setminus Z$ ($i\geq 1$) converging to $z$ such that \[  \lim _{i	o \infty } \varphi (x_ i)=\infty .  \] Using ( 9.10.15 ) around each $x_ i$, we may further assume that $x_ i\in X\setminus (\Phi ^{-1}(\Phi (Z)\cup V))$. Let $L$ be a complex line passing through $\Phi (z)$ intersecting $(\Phi (Z)\cup V)\cap \overline{B}$ only at $\Phi (z)$, where $B\Subset B'\Subset \Omega $ are two small open balls centered at $\Phi (z)$. Since $\Phi $ is finite, $\Phi (Z)$ still has codimension at least $2$ in $\Omega $. Hence, for each $i$, the set of directions of lines through $\Phi (x_ i)$ meeting $B'\cap \Phi (Z)$ is contained in a proper analytic subset of the projective space of directions. We can therefore choose lines $L_ i$ through $\Phi (x_ i)$ converging to $L$ such that $L_ i\cap (B'\cap \Phi (Z))=\varnothing $. Moreover, since $\Phi (x_ i)
otin V$, no such $L_ i$ is contained in $V$, and hence $L_ i\cap (B'\cap V)$ is discrete. Then $\Phi $ restricts to a branched covering over $B'\cap L_ i$ for all $i\geq 1$. Adding a constant to $\varphi $, we may assume that $\varphi |_{\Phi ^{-1}(L\cap \partial B)}<0$. We can then find an open neighborhood $U$ of $\Phi ^{-1}(L\cap \partial B)$ so that $\varphi |_ U<0$. For large $i$, we have $\Phi ^{-1}(L_ i\cap \partial B)\subseteq U$ and $\Phi (x_ i)\in B$. Put \[  C_ i\coloneqq \Phi ^{-1}(L_ i\cap B').  \] Thus $C_ i$ is a one-dimensional complex space contained in $X\setminus Z$. Since $\Phi |_{C_ i}$ is finite over $L_ i\cap B'$, the inverse image $C_ i\cap \Phi ^{-1}(\overline B)$ is compact, and its boundary is contained in $\Phi ^{-1}(L_ i\cap \partial B)$. Passing to the normalization of each irreducible component of $C_ i$, the pull-back of $\varphi $ is subharmonic. The one-dimensional maximum principle therefore gives \[  \varphi (x_ i)\leq \sup _{\Phi ^{-1}(L_ i\cap \partial B)}\varphi <0,  \] which is a contradiction. $\square$

title: Corollary 9.10.16
text: Corollary 9.10.16 . 2DA8FD7B7A99 Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism between compact Kähler spaces. Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Assume that $X$ is unibranch. Then the pull-back induces a bijection \[  \pi ^*\colon \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\xlongrightarrow {\sim }\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta ).  \] Proof. Injectivity follows from the surjectivity of $\pi $. For surjectivity, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta )$. The assertion is local on $X$, so after subtracting a local potential of $\theta $ we may assume that $\theta =0$. By theorem 9.10.5 , the fibers of $\pi $ are connected. The restriction of $u$ to any compact fiber is psh, hence is constant by the maximum principle. Thus $u$ descends to a function $v$ on $X$. Since $\pi $ is proper, $v$ is upper semicontinuous. It remains to check that $v$ is psh. By theorem 9.10.13 , it suffices to test on holomorphic disks. Let $f\colon \Delta \rightarrow X$ be a holomorphic disk such that $f^*v\not\equiv -\infty $. As in the proof of theorem 9.10.14 , after a finite ramified cover $\rho \colon \Delta \rightarrow \Delta $, the germ of $f\circ \rho $ lifts to $Y$. The pull-back $(f^*v)\circ \rho $ is therefore subharmonic, so $f^*v$ is subharmonic. Hence $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, and the general $\theta $-psh case follows by adding back the local potentials. $\square$

title: 9.10.17 Extensions of the results in the smooth setting
search_title: Extensions of the results in the smooth setting
text: Let $X$ be an irreducible unibranch compact Kähler space of dimension $n$. Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. We say the cohomology class $\{ \theta \} $ is big if for any proper bimeromorphic morphism $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ from a compact Kähler manifold $Y$, $\{ \pi ^*\theta \} $ is big. This definition is independent of the choice of $\pi $. The non-pluripolar products can be defined exactly as in section 13.1 and the results in that chapter hold mutatis mutandis . The results in section 16.1 can also be easily extended. The definition of the $P$-envelope remains unchanged. As for the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope, we define Definition 9.10.18 . 3BD14AE7D7C8 Given $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we define $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ as the unique element with the following property: If $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ is a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a compact Kähler manifold $Y$, then \[  \pi ^*P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\pi ^*\theta }[\pi ^*\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] It follows from corollary 9.10.16 and proposition 16.6.10 that $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ is independent of the choice of $\pi $ and is well-defined. The other results can be easily extended. section 17.10 and section 16.7 can be extended without big changes. The only exception is theorem 16.9.59 , where we do not have the notion of multiplier ideal sheaves. So we do not know how to extend this theorem. section 18.1 can be extended except for subsection 18.1.44 for the same reason as above. If $Y\subseteq X$ is an irreducible analytic subspace not contained in $X^{\operatorname{Sing}}$, then the trace operator of section 20.2 can be extended to this setting by using an embedded resolution. In general, due to the lack of Demailly regularization on singular spaces, we do not know how to define the trace operator. section 17.11 can be easily extended. section 19.1 is easy to extend since the partial Okounkov bodies are bimeromorphically invariant in the sense of theorem 19.5.26 . section 20.1 is unchanged, since we always take projective limits with respect to all models in that section. section 21.13 can be extended using the toric resolution [ Theorem 11.1.9 , CLS11 ] . section 22.1 can be extended except for the parts involving the trace operator. section 18.28 can be easily extended by considering a resolution.
